9	---
10	
11	# Relational Algebra and SQL
12	
13	**Relational algebra (RA)** is the procedural mathematical foundation for querying relational databases. It defines *how* to retrieve data. **SQL** is the declarative language that sits on top — it defines *what* to retrieve, and the DBMS's query optimiser translates it into an efficient RA execution plan.
14	
15	> RA is to DBMS what machine code is to a CPU — the internal execution language.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Relational Algebra
20	
21	### Fundamental Operators (6)
22	
23	All RA queries can be expressed using these six operators alone.
24	
25	#### 1. Select — σ (tuple-wise filter)
26	
27	```
28	σ_P(r)
29	```
30	
31	Returns all tuples in relation `r` where predicate `P` is true.  
32	Logical operators: `∧` (AND), `∨` (OR), `¬` (NOT).  
33	Comparison: `=`, `≠`, `<`, `>`, `≤`, `≥`.
34	
35	```
36	σ_{location="Winterfell" ∧ YOB>285}(GOT)
37	```
38	
39	SQL equivalent: `SELECT * FROM r WHERE P`
40	
41	#### 2. Project — π (column-wise selection)
42	
43	```
44	π_{a,b,...}(r)
45	```
46	
47	Returns only the specified columns. Duplicate tuples are **eliminated** (RA operates on sets).
48	
49	```
50	π_{Location}(GOT)   -- returns distinct locations
51	```
52	
53	SQL equivalent: `SELECT DISTINCT a, b FROM r`
54	
55	#### 3. Set Union — ∪
56	
57	```
58	r ∪ s
59	```
60	
61	Returns all tuples from both relations, removing duplicates.  
62	**Requirement**: `r` and `s` must have the same schema (same attribute names, types, and order).
63	
64	#### 4. Set Difference — −
65	
66	```
67	r − s
68	```
69	
70	Returns tuples in `r` that are *not* in `s`. Note: `r − s ≠ s − r`.  
71	**Requirement**: same schema as union.
72	
73	#### 5. Cartesian Product — ×
74	
75	```
76	r × s
77	```
78	
79	Returns all combinations of tuples from `r` and `s` (n_r × n_s tuples).  
80	If both have attribute `id`, they become `r.id` and `s.id`.  
81	No schema constraint — unlike union and difference.
82	
83	#### 6. Rename — ρ
84	
85	```
86	ρ_x(E)               -- rename relation E as x
87	ρ_{x(a1,a2,...)}(E)  -- rename relation and attributes
88	```
89	
90	Used to: refer to intermediate results, resolve ambiguities, and self-join (`r × ρ_s(r)`).
91	
92	---
93	
94	### Extended Operators
95	
96	These can be expressed using the fundamental six, but are provided for convenience.
97	
98	#### Intersection — ∩
99	
100	```
101	r ∩ s  ≡  r − (r − s)
102	```
103	
104	Returns tuples present in both relations. Same schema requirement as union.
105	
106	#### Natural Join — ⋈
107	
108	```
109	r ⋈ s
110	```
111	
112	Joins on *all common attributes* (same name and type), returning one copy of the common columns.
113	
114	```
115	r ⋈ s  ≡  π_{S∪T}(σ_{r.A1=s.A1 ∧ … ∧ r.Am=s.Am}(r × s))
116	```
117	
118	where `S ∩ T = {A1, …, Am}` are the shared attributes.
119	
120	#### Outer Joins
121	
122	Handle "imperfect" matches by padding with NULL instead of discarding non-matching tuples:
123	
124	| Operator | Symbol | Behaviour |
125	|----------|--------|-----------|
126	| **Left outer join** | r ⟕ s | Keep all tuples from `r`; fill missing `s` attributes with NULL |
127	| **Right outer join** | r ⟖ s | Keep all tuples from `s`; fill missing `r` attributes with NULL |
128	| **Full outer join** | r ⟗ s | Keep all tuples from both; fill missing values with NULL |
129	
130	#### Division — ÷
131	
132	```
133	r ÷ s
134	```
135	
136	Used for "for all" queries. Returns tuples in `r` associated with *every* tuple in `s`.  
137	Requirement: attributes of `s` are a subset of attributes of `r`.
138	
139	```
140	-- Find modules taught in ALL programmes
141	Modules(module, programme) ÷ AllProgrammes(programme)
142	```
143	
144	#### Assignment — ←
145	
146	Stores an intermediate result in a temporary variable:
147	
148	```
149	r1 ← σ_{color='red'}(Parts)
150	r2 ← r1 ⋈ Catalog
151	```
152	
153	Equivalent to SQL CTEs or subqueries. Cuts complex queries into readable steps.
154	
155	---
156	
157	### Query Efficiency in RA
158	
159	**Key principle**: push selections and projections *before* joins to reduce tuple counts early.
160	
161	```
162	-- Inefficient: join everything, then filter
163	π_{name,title}(σ_{dept='ICT'}(instructor ⋈ teaches ⋈ course))
164	
165	-- Efficient: filter instructor first, then join smaller set
166	π_{name,title}(σ_{dept='ICT'}(instructor) ⋈ teaches ⋈ π_{course_id,title}(course))
167	```
168	
169	---
170	
171	## SQL
172	
173	SQL is the universal declarative query language for relational databases. Standardised in 1986 (ANSI), revised through SQL:2019.
174	
175	### SQL Sublanguages
176	
177	| Sublanguage | Commands | Purpose |
178	|-------------|----------|---------|
179	| **DDL** (Data Definition) | `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` | Define and modify schema |
180	| **DML** (Data Manipulation) | `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` | Manipulate data |
181	| **DCL** (Data Control) | `GRANT`, `REVOKE` | Access control |
182	| **TCL** (Transaction Control) | `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT` | Transaction management |
183	
184	---
185	
186	### DDL: Defining Schema
187	
188	```sql
189	CREATE TABLE Sailors (
190	    sid     INTEGER,
191	    name    CHAR(10),
192	    rating  INTEGER,
193	    age     INTEGER,
194	    PRIMARY KEY (sid),
195	    CHECK (rating >= 1 AND rating <= 10)
196	);
197	
198	-- Modify table structure
199	ALTER TABLE Sailors ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100);
200	ALTER TABLE Sailors DROP COLUMN email;
201	
202	-- Remove table
203	DROP TABLE Sailors;
204	```
205	
206	**Common data types:**
207	
208	| Type | Description |
209	|------|-------------|
210	| `INT` / `SMALLINT` | Integer values |
211	| `NUMERIC(p,d)` | Fixed-point: p total digits, d after decimal |
212	| `REAL` / `DOUBLE PRECISION` | Floating-point |
213	| `CHAR(n)` | Fixed-length string of n characters |
214	| `VARCHAR(n)` | Variable-length string, max n characters |
215	| `DATE` / `TIME` / `TIMESTAMP` | Temporal values |
216	
217	---
218	
219	### DML: Manipulating Data
220	
221	#### INSERT
222	
223	```sql
224	-- Full row (column order must match schema)
225	INSERT INTO Sailors VALUES (74, 'Rusty', 7.5, 35);
226	
227	-- Partial row (specify columns explicitly)
228	INSERT INTO Sailors (sid, name, rating) VALUES (75, 'Sandy', 8);
229	```
230	
231	#### UPDATE
232	
233	```sql
234	UPDATE Sailors
235	SET rating = 9.5
236	WHERE sid = 22;
237	```
238	
239	#### DELETE
240	
241	```sql
242	DELETE FROM Sailors
243	WHERE sid = 74;
244	```
245	
246	#### SELECT
247	
248	The most important SQL statement. General form:
249	
250	```sql
251	SELECT   col1, col2, ...       -- π (project): which columns
252	FROM     table1, table2, ...   -- relations (implicit cross product)
253	WHERE    condition              -- σ (select): filter tuples
254	GROUP BY attributes            -- partition into groups
255	HAVING   group_condition       -- filter groups
256	ORDER BY attributes [ASC|DESC];-- sort result
257	```
258	
259	- `SELECT *` returns all columns  
260	- `SELECT DISTINCT` removes duplicates (costly; avoid unless needed)  
261	- SQL operates on **multi-sets** (bags); RA operates on sets — duplicates are retained unless `DISTINCT` is used
262	
263	**Arithmetic and aliases:**
264	
265	```sql
266	SELECT sid, name, rating / 2 AS new_rating, age
267	FROM Sailors;
268	```
269	
270	**Multi-table queries (implicit join via WHERE):**
271	
272	```sql
273	-- Find names of sailors who reserved a red boat
274	SELECT S.name
275	FROM Sailors S, Reserves R, Boats B
276	WHERE S.sid = R.sid
277	  AND R.bid = B.bid
278	  AND B.color = 'red';
279	```
280	
281	**Explicit JOIN syntax:**
282	
283	```sql
284	SELECT S.name, B.color
285	FROM Sailors S
286	INNER JOIN Reserves R ON S.sid = R.sid
287	INNER JOIN Boats B    ON R.bid = B.bid
288	WHERE B.color = 'red';
289	
290	-- Left outer join (keep unmatched left rows)
291	SELECT S.name, R.bid
292	FROM Sailors S
293	LEFT JOIN Reserves R ON S.sid = R.sid;
294	```
295	
296	---
297	
298	### Set Operations
299	
300	```sql
301	-- UNION (removes duplicates by default)
302	SELECT name FROM Sailors WHERE rating = 10
303	UNION
304	SELECT name FROM Sailors WHERE age < 20;
305	
306	-- UNION ALL (retains duplicates; faster)
307	SELECT Name FROM Finance
308	UNION ALL
309	SELECT Name FROM HR;
310	
311	-- INTERSECT (common tuples)
312	SELECT S1.name FROM Sailors S1, Boats B1, Reserves R1
313	WHERE S1.sid = R1.sid AND R1.bid = B1.bid AND B1.color = 'red'
314	INTERSECT
315	SELECT S2.name FROM Sailors S2, Boats B2, Reserves R2
316	WHERE S2.sid = R2.sid AND R2.bid = B2.bid AND B2.color = 'green';
317	
318	-- EXCEPT / MINUS (set difference)
319	SELECT sid FROM Reserves WHERE bid IN (SELECT bid FROM Boats WHERE color = 'red')
320	EXCEPT
321	SELECT sid FROM Reserves WHERE bid IN (SELECT bid FROM Boats WHERE color = 'green');
322	```
323	
324	---
325	
326	### Aggregate Functions
327	
328	```sql
329	SELECT COUNT(*)          FROM Sailors;               -- row count
330	SELECT AVG(age)          FROM Sailors WHERE rating > 8.5;
331	SELECT MIN(age), MAX(age) FROM Sailors;
332	SELECT SUM(salary)       FROM Employees;
333	SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT rating) FROM Sailors;          -- distinct values
334	```
335	
336	**Rules:**
337	- If `SELECT` uses an aggregate, it must *only* contain aggregates — unless `GROUP BY` is used
338	- Cannot use aggregates in `WHERE` — use a subquery or `HAVING` instead
339	
340	---
341	
342	### GROUP BY and HAVING
343	
344	```sql
345	SELECT rating, AVG(age) AS avg_age
346	FROM Sailors
347	GROUP BY rating
348	HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;   -- only groups with more than 1 sailor
349	```
350	
351	**Evaluation order:**
352	1. `FROM` + `WHERE` — filter tuples
353	2. `GROUP BY` — partition into groups
354	3. `HAVING` — filter groups
355	4. `SELECT` — compute output per group
356	5. `ORDER BY` — sort
357	
358	**NULL in aggregation**: NULL is *ignored* in aggregation functions. `COUNT(*)` counts all rows; `COUNT(col)` ignores NULLs. `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` all skip NULLs.
359	
360	---
361	
362	### Subqueries (Nested Queries)
363	
364	```sql
365	-- Correlated subquery in WHERE
366	SELECT S.name
367	FROM Sailors S
368	WHERE S.sid IN (
369	    SELECT R.sid FROM Reserves R WHERE R.bid = 103
370	);
371	
372	-- Scalar subquery
373	SELECT S1.name, S1.age
374	FROM Sailors S1
375	WHERE S1.age = (SELECT MAX(S2.age) FROM Sailors S2);
376	```
377	
378	**Set comparison operators:**
379	
380	| Operator | Meaning |
381	|----------|---------|
382	| `IN` | Value is in the set (= ANY) |
383	| `NOT IN` | Value is not in the set (<> ALL) |
384	| `> ANY` / `> SOME` | Greater than at least one value in the set |
385	| `> ALL` | Greater than every value in the set |
386	| `EXISTS (...)` | Subquery returns at least one row |
387	| `NOT EXISTS (...)` | Subquery returns no rows |
388	
389	**`EXISTS` vs `IN`**: prefer `EXISTS` when checking membership — it short-circuits on the first match rather than scanning the entire subquery result.
390	
391	---
392	
393	### Special Values and Operators
394	
395	**NULL:**
396	```sql
397	WHERE age IS NULL        -- correct
398	WHERE age IS NOT NULL    -- correct
399	-- WHERE age = NULL      -- WRONG — always evaluates to NULL, never TRUE
400	```
401	
402	**LIKE (pattern matching):**
403	```sql
404	WHERE name LIKE 'Ja%'    -- starts with 'Ja'
405	WHERE name LIKE '_i%'    -- second character is 'i'
406	WHERE name LIKE 'J\_%'   -- literal underscore (escaped)
407	```
408	Avoid leading wildcards (`'%abc'`) — cannot use an index.
409	
410	**ORDER BY:**
411	```sql
412	ORDER BY rating ASC, age DESC   -- sort by rating ascending, then age descending
413	ORDER BY A + B DESC              -- can use expressions
414	```
415	
416	---
417	
418	### CHECK Constraints
419	
420	```sql
421	-- Attribute-level (checked on INSERT/UPDATE of that attribute)
422	CREATE TABLE Sailors (
423	    sid    INTEGER,
424	    rating INTEGER CHECK (rating >= 1 AND rating <= 10),
425	    age    INTEGER CHECK (age > 0)
426	);
427	
428	-- Tuple-level (checked whenever any attribute of the tuple changes)
429	CHECK (rating >= 1 AND rating <= 10 AND age > 0)
430	
431	-- Domain definition with CHECK
432	CREATE DOMAIN rtval INTEGER DEFAULT 1
433	    CHECK (VALUE >= 1 AND VALUE <= 10);
434	```
435	
436	---
437	
438	### SQL Query Optimisation Tips
439	
440	| Tip | Why |
441	|-----|-----|
442	| `SELECT col1, col2` instead of `SELECT *` | Avoids transferring unnecessary data |
443	| Avoid `SELECT DISTINCT` unless required | Duplicate elimination is expensive |
444	| Use `UNION ALL` instead of `UNION` when duplicates are acceptable | `UNION` must de-duplicate |
445	| Keep wildcards at the **end** of `LIKE` patterns (`'Ram%'`, not `'%Ram%'`) | Leading `%` cannot use an index |
446	| Use `EXISTS` instead of `COUNT(*) > 0` | `EXISTS` stops at first match |
447	| Replace correlated subqueries with `JOIN` + `GROUP BY` | Joins are processed once; correlated subqueries re-execute per row |
448	| Choose the correct JOIN type | Avoid implicit cross-products; use `INNER JOIN` with an `ON` condition |
449	| Use indexes on `WHERE`, `JOIN ON`, and `ORDER BY` columns | See [[concepts/database-indexing-transactions]] |
450	
451	---
452	
453	## See Also
454	
455	- [[concepts/relational-database-fundamentals]] — Relational model, keys, integrity constraints
456	- [[concepts/database-normalisation]] — FDs and schema refinement using RA theory
457	- [[concepts/database-indexing-transactions]] — How the DBMS implements RA operators efficiently
458	- [[concepts/er-diagrams]] — Conceptual design that produces the schemas queried here

9	---
10	
11	# Database Normalisation
12	
13	Normalisation is the process of designing a consistent database schema with *minimum redundancy*. It is Stage 4 (Schema Refinement) of the six-stage database design process — applied after the initial relational schema has been derived from an ER diagram.
14	
15	> **Goal**: capture all necessary information with as little stored redundancy as possible.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## Why Normalise? — Data Anomalies
20	
21	A poorly designed table that stores unrelated information together introduces **anomalies** — problems that arise when the data is modified.
22	
23	**Example poorly designed table:**
24	
25	| SID | Sname | ModuleID | ModuleName | Fee |
26	|-----|-------|----------|------------|-----|
27	| S1  | A     | M1       | C++        | 500 |
28	| S2  | B     | M1       | C++        | 500 |
29	| S3  | C     | M2       | Java       | 400 |
30	
31	| Anomaly | Symptom |
32	|---------|---------|
33	| **Insertion anomaly** | Cannot record a new module (e.g., Python) without first enrolling a student |
34	| **Redundancy anomaly** | Module name and fee are repeated for every enrolled student |
35	| **Update anomaly** | Changing the fee for M1 requires updating *every* tuple where M1 appears — inconsistency if any row is missed |
36	| **Deletion anomaly** | Deleting student S3 also destroys all information about module M2 |
37	
38	**Solution: decomposition** — split the table into smaller, non-redundant relations.
39	
40	---
41	
42	## Functional Dependencies (FDs)
43	
44	A **functional dependency** X → Y means: knowing the value of X is sufficient to determine the value of Y.
45	
46	> For any two tuples t1 and t2 in relation R: if t1[X] = t2[X] then t1[Y] = t2[Y].
47	
48	**Notation**: `EmpID → Name, Phone, Position` (EmpID determines Name, Phone, and Position)
49	
50	**Key distinctions:**
51	- An FD is a *constraint on all possible legal instances* of the relation — not just the current one
52	- Looking at one instance can show that an FD *does not* hold; it cannot prove that an FD *does* hold
53	- FDs generalise key constraints: if `K → all attributes`, then K is a superkey; the reverse is not necessarily true
54	
55	---
56	
57	## Armstrong's Axioms
58	
59	A **sound and complete** set of inference rules for deriving all FDs from a given set F.
60	
61	Let X, Y, Z denote sets of attributes.
62	
63	| Rule | Statement |
64	|------|-----------|
65	| **Reflexivity** | If X ⊆ Y, then Y → X |
66	| **Augmentation** | If X → Y, then XZ → YZ for any Z |
67	| **Transitivity** | If X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z |
68	
69	**Derived rules** (provable from the three axioms):
70	
71	| Rule | Statement | Proof sketch |
72	|------|-----------|-------------|
73	| **Union** | If X → Y and X → Z, then X → YZ | Augmentation + Transitivity |
74	| **Decomposition** | If X → YZ, then X → Y and X → Z | Reflexivity + Transitivity |
75	| **Pseudo-transitivity** | If X → Y and YZ → U, then XZ → U | Augmentation + Transitivity |
76	
77	---
78	
79	## Attribute Closure (X⁺)
80	
81	The **closure of a set of attributes X** with respect to a set of FDs F is the complete set of attributes functionally determined by X.
82	
83	**Algorithm:**
84	
85	```
86	Input:  attribute set X, FD set F
87	Output: X⁺
88	
89	1. Split all FDs so each has a single attribute on the right-hand side.
90	2. Result := X
91	3. Repeat until no change:
92	       for each FD B → Y in F:
93	           if B ⊆ Result then Result := Result ∪ {Y}
94	4. X⁺ := Result
95	```
96	
97	**Example:**
98	
99	FDs: `name → color`, `category → department`, `{color, category} → price`  
100	Compute `{name, category}⁺`:
101	
102	1. X = {name, category}
103	2. `name → color` → add color → X = {name, category, color}
104	3. `category → department` → add department → X = {name, category, color, department}
105	4. `{color, category} → price` → both in X → add price → X = {name, category, color, department, price}
106	
107	`{name, category}⁺` = {name, category, color, department, price}
108	
109	### Uses of Closure
110	
111	| Question | How to Answer |
112	|----------|--------------|
113	| Is X → Y derivable from F? | Compute X⁺; check whether Y ⊆ X⁺ |
114	| What are the keys of R? | Find subsets K where K⁺ = all attributes of R |
115	| Are FD sets F and G equivalent? | Check every FD in F is derivable from G, and vice versa |
116	
117	---
118	
119	## Normal Forms
120	
121	Normal forms are benchmarks that characterise how well-designed a schema is. Each higher form eliminates a further class of anomaly.
122	
123	```
124	Unnormalised  →  1NF  →  2NF  →  3NF  →  BCNF  →  4NF  →  5NF
125	Most redundancy                                          Least redundancy
126	```
127	
128	For most practical purposes, **BCNF is the target**.
129	
130	### 1NF — First Normal Form
131	
132	> All attribute values are **atomic** (indivisible). No multi-valued cells, no lists.
133	
134	**Violation:**
135	
136	| Name | GPA | Courses |
137	|------|-----|---------|
138	| Alice | 3.8 | Math; DB; OS |
139	
140	**Fix:** Split multi-valued attribute into a separate linking table.
141	
142	| Name | GPA | | Name | Course |
143	|------|-----|-|------|--------|
144	| Alice | 3.8 | | Alice | Math |
145	| Bob | 3.7 | | Alice | DB |
146	| | | | Alice | OS |
147	
148	### BCNF — Boyce-Codd Normal Form
149	
150	> For every non-trivial FD X → Y in relation R, X must be a **superkey** of R.
151	
152	**A trivial FD** is one where Y ⊆ X (e.g., `{A, B} → A`).
153	
154	**Test:** Compute X⁺ for each non-trivial FD. If X⁺ ≠ all attributes of R, the FD violates BCNF.
155	
156	**Example violation:**
157	
158	```
159	Product(name, price, category, color)
160	FDs: {name, category} → price, category → color
161	
162	(name, category)⁺ = {name, category, price, color}  ← superkey ✓
163	category⁺         = {category, color}               ← NOT a superkey ✗
164	```
165	
166	`Product` is NOT in BCNF because `category → color` has a non-superkey left-hand side.
167	
168	---
169	
170	## BCNF Decomposition Algorithm
171	
172	**Cannot** arbitrarily split relations — must use the violating FD to guide decomposition.
173	
174	```
175	Normalise(R):
176	    Find FD X → A in R where A ∉ X and X⁺ ≠ all attributes (violates BCNF)
177	    If none found: R is in BCNF. Return.
178	    Else:
179	        Y = X⁺ − X       (attributes determined by X, excluding X itself)
180	        Z = R − X⁺       (remaining attributes not determined by X)
181	        Decompose R into R1(X⁺) and R2(X ∪ Z)
182	        Recursively Normalise(R1) and Normalise(R2)
183	```
184	
185	**Example 1:**
186	
187	```
188	Person(Name, SSN, Age, HairColour, PhoneNo)
189	FDs: SSN → Name, Age, HairColour
190	     Age → HairColour
191	
192	Iteration 1: SSN⁺ = {SSN, Name, Age, HairColour} ← bad FD
193	  → Decompose: P(SSN, Name, Age, HairColour) and Phone(SSN, PhoneNo)
194	
195	Iteration 2: check P — Age⁺ = {Age, HairColour} ← bad FD
196	  → Decompose P: People(SSN, Name, Age) and Hair(Age, HairColour)
197	
198	Final: People(SSN, Name, Age), Hair(Age, HairColour), Phone(SSN, PhoneNo)
199	```
200	
201	---
202	
203	## Properties of Decomposition
204	
205	After decomposing R into R1 and R2, two properties must be evaluated:
206	
207	### Lossless Join (BCNF guarantees this ✓)
208	
209	A decomposition of R into S and T is **lossless** if and only if:
210	
211	```
212	S ∩ T ≠ ∅   AND   R = S ⋈ T
213	```
214	
215	The original relation can be perfectly reconstructed by natural-joining the decomposed relations. BCNF decomposition always produces a lossless join.
216	
217	**Lossy example:** Decomposing `Person(Name, Power, Category)` into `{Name, Power}` and `{Name, Category}` loses the `Power–Category` association — the join produces spurious tuples.
218	
219	### Dependency Preservation (BCNF does NOT guarantee this ✗)
220	
221	A decomposition **preserves all FDs** if every original FD can be enforced by checking constraints on individual decomposed relations (without joining).
222	
223	BCNF can violate this:
224	
225	```
226	R(C, P, S, J, D, Q)
227	FDs: C → PSJDQ, JP → C, SD → P, J → S
228	Decompose into: R1(CJDQ), R2(JS), R3(SDP)
229	
230	JP → C spans R1 and R2 — cannot be enforced without joining.
231	```
232	
233	**Trade-off:** If dependency preservation is critical, add a relation `(J, P, C)` solely to enforce `JP → C` — accepting some redundancy.
234	
235	---
236	
237	## Normalisation vs. Performance
238	
239	Normalisation reduces redundancy but can *increase* query cost — joins are expensive.
240	
241	| Approach | Benefit | Cost |
242	|----------|---------|------|
243	| Fully normalised | No redundancy, easy updates | More joins required for queries |
244	| Intentionally denormalised | Faster reads (one table, no join) | Redundancy; update anomalies |
245	
246	> **Design principle**: normalise first; denormalise selectively based on measured query performance.
247	
248	A database designer may deliberately keep a "bad" (denormalised) relation for performance-critical read paths — but the trade-off must be consciously accepted.
249	
250	---
251	
252	## Summary: The Normalisation Story
253	
254	```
255	Bad design → anomalies
256	Anomalies  → redundancy
257	Redundancy → decomposition guided by FDs
258	FDs        → Armstrong's axioms → closure → BCNF check
259	BCNF       → lossless decomposition (but may sacrifice dependency preservation)
260	Resulting schema: minimal redundancy, no update/insert/delete anomalies
261	```
262	
263	---
264	
265	## See Also
266	
267	- [[concepts/relational-database-fundamentals]] — Keys and integrity constraints (FDs generalise key constraints)
268	- [[concepts/er-diagrams]] — S2–S3 of design; normalisation is S4
269	- [[concepts/relational-algebra-and-sql]] — SQL used to implement and query normalised schemas
270	- [[sources/INF2003-database-systems]] — Source course

9	---
10	
11	# Database Indexing and Transactions
12	
13	This page covers the physical layer (Stage S5) and security/recovery layer (Stage S6) of the database design process — specifically: how the DBMS stores and retrieves data efficiently (indexing), and how it maintains correctness under concurrent access and failures (transactions).
14	
15	---
16	
17	## File Organisation
18	
19	A table is stored in a **data file** made up of **pages** (fixed-size chunks). How pages are organised determines query performance.
20	
21	| Organisation | Description | Best For |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| **Heap file** | Pages in arbitrary order; tuples unsorted | Full table scans (`SELECT *`) |
24	| **Sorted file** | Pages sorted by one or more attributes | Range queries and ORDER BY |
25	| **Index** | Additional data structure alongside the file | Point queries and range queries on the indexed attribute |
26	
27	**Creating an index in SQL:**
28	```sql
29	CREATE INDEX idx_sid ON Students (sid);
30	```
31	
32	**Trade-off:** Indexes speed up reads (`SELECT`) but slow down writes (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) because the index must be maintained on every modification. Create indexes strategically on columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN ON`, and `ORDER BY`.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## Index Data Structures
37	
38	### Hash Index
39	
40	Uses a **hash function** `h(r)` to map a record's search key to a **bucket** (primary page + optional overflow pages).
41	
42	```
43	h(r) = bucket number → scan that bucket for the record
44	```
45	
46	**Properties:**
47	- O(1) average for equality search: `WHERE sid = '2001234'`
48	- **Cannot** support range queries: `WHERE year BETWEEN 2013 AND 2015` — hash destroys ordering
49	- One record belongs to exactly one bucket; different records may share a bucket (collision)
50	
51	**Use when:** You need only equality lookups; key distribution is fairly uniform.
52	
53	---
54	
55	### B+ Tree
56	
57	The most widely used index structure in relational DBMS. Supports both equality and range queries.
58	
59	**Structure:**
60	- **Root node** — top of the tree
61	- **Internal nodes** — routing nodes containing keys and pointers to children
62	- **Leaf nodes** — all data entries; leaves are linked together in a doubly-linked list
63	
64	**Key invariants:**
65	- All data is in the **leaf** nodes (internal nodes only route)
66	- All leaves are at the **same level** (perfectly balanced)
67	- Each leaf node contains `k` keys and `k+1` pointers, with **minimum 50% occupancy** (root is exempt)
68	- **High fanout** (typically 100+): each internal node has many children → shallow tree → few I/Os per search
69	
70	---
71	
72	#### B+ Tree: Search — O(log n)
73	
74	Traverse from root to leaf following key comparisons.
75	
76	**Range search** `[8, 24]`:
77	1. Search for lower bound (8) → land on a leaf
78	2. Follow the linked leaf list until the upper bound (24) is passed
79	
80	Hash cannot do this; B+ tree can in O(log n + k) where k is the number of results.
81	
82	---
83	
84	#### B+ Tree: Insert
85	
86	1. **Locate** the target leaf
87	2. **Insert** the key
88	   - If the leaf has space: done
89	   - If the leaf is full: **split** the leaf into two; duplicate the minimum key of the second node into the parent
90	3. **Recursively** propagate splits up the tree if the parent is also full
91	4. If the root splits, a **new root** is created — the tree grows taller
92	
93	**Example: insert 8 into a leaf `[2, 3, 5, 7]` (capacity 4)**
94	1. Leaf is full → split: `[2, 3]` and `[5, 7, 8]`
95	2. Duplicate `5` into parent → parent may also split → recurse
96	
97	---
98	
99	#### B+ Tree: Delete
100	
101	1. **Locate** the target leaf; remove the key
102	2. If the leaf still meets minimum occupancy: done
103	3. If **under-full**:
104	   - Try **borrowing** from the nearest sibling (left sibling preferred)
105	   - If borrowing is not possible (sibling is also at minimum): **merge** the two siblings into one node and remove the separator key from the parent
106	4. **Recursively** propagate merges up the tree
107	5. If the root becomes empty, the tree shrinks in height
108	
109	A B+ tree is a **dynamic structure**: it grows and shrinks gracefully without periodic reorganisation.
110	
111	**Complexity summary:**
112	
113	| Operation | Time |
114	|-----------|------|
115	| Search (point) | O(log n) |
116	| Search (range) | O(log n + k) |
117	| Insert | O(log n) |
118	| Delete | O(log n) |
119	
120	---
121	
122	## Transactions
123	
124	A **transaction (TXN)** is a logical unit of work: a sequence of database reads and writes that must execute as a single, indivisible operation.
125	
126	**Example — bank transfer:**
127	1. Read `bal_wei`
128	2. Write `bal_wei := bal_wei − 100`
129	3. Read `bal_wayne`
130	4. Write `bal_wayne := bal_wayne + 100`
131	
132	If step 2 completes but step 4 fails, the money disappears. Transactions prevent this.
133	
134	---
135	
136	## ACID Properties (Deep Dive)
137	
138	| Property | Guarantee | Who is Responsible |
139	|----------|-----------|-------------------|
140	| **Atomicity** | All operations execute, or none do. No partial commits. | DBMS (transaction manager) |
141	| **Consistency** | Database moves from one consistent state to another. ICs hold before and after. | Application programmer |
142	| **Isolation** | Concurrently executing transactions appear to each other as if they were serial. | DBMS (concurrency control) |
143	| **Durability** | Once committed, changes survive system crashes. | DBMS (recovery manager) |
144	
145	**Consistency nuance:** ACID consistency means ICs are satisfied — not that the *business logic* is correct. If you mistakenly code a 30% interest rate instead of 3%, ACID cannot detect that.
146	
147	---
148	
149	## Schedules and Serializability
150	
151	A **schedule** is an ordered sequence of operations from multiple concurrent transactions.
152	
153	| Schedule Type | Description | Safety |
154	|---|---|---|
155	| **Serial** | All operations of T1 complete before T2 starts; no interleaving | Safe; often poor performance |
156	| **Equivalent** | Two schedules that produce the same output | — |
157	| **Serializable** | Equivalent to *some* serial schedule | Safe |
158	
159	**Goal:** allow interleaved execution (for performance) while guaranteeing serializability (for correctness).
160	
161	**Interleaving can cause problems:**
162	
163	| Problem | Description |
164	|---------|-------------|
165	| **Dirty read** | T1 reads data written by T2 before T2 commits; T2 then rolls back |
166	| **Non-repeatable read** | T1 reads a value twice; T2 modifies it between the two reads |
167	| **Lost update** | T1 and T2 both read and then overwrite the same value; one update is lost |
168	
169	---
170	
171	## SQL Transaction Control (TCL)
172	
173	```sql
174	-- Mark a savepoint
175	SAVEPOINT sp1234;
176	
177	-- Undo all changes since sp1234
178	ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1234;
179	
180	-- Make all pending changes permanent
181	COMMIT;
182	
183	-- Discard all pending changes
184	ROLLBACK;
185	```
186	
187	**A transaction ends with `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, or a DDL/DCL statement.**
188	
189	```sql
190	-- Example: safe update with savepoint
191	UPDATE Students SET grade = 'B' WHERE sid = 200123;
192	SAVEPOINT sp1234;
193	INSERT INTO Students VALUES (200999, 'Jon', 'A');
194	UPDATE Students SET grade = 'A+';   -- oops — updates ALL rows
195	ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1234;       -- undo the bad UPDATE; keep the grade='B' change
196	COMMIT;                             -- commit the grade='B' UPDATE
197	```
198	
199	---
200	
201	## Concurrency Control
202	
203	### Locking
204	
205	The simplest correctness mechanism: before accessing data, a transaction acquires a lock.
206	
207	**Lock granularity** (from coarsest to finest):
208	
209	| Level | Scope | Suitability |
210	|-------|-------|-------------|
211	| Database | Entire database | Single-user only |
212	| Table | Entire table | Low concurrency |
213	| Page | One disk page | Most practical for multi-user |
214	| Row | One row | High concurrency; many locks |
215	| Field | One column of one row | Rarely used; impractical overhead |
216	
217	**Deadlock**: T1 waits for T2 to release a lock; T2 waits for T1. Neither can proceed.  
218	Prevention: careful lock ordering in code. Detection: timeout; the DBMS kills one transaction and rolls it back.
219	
220	### Optimistic Concurrency Control (3-Phase Method)
221	
222	When write conflicts are rare, the cost of locking outweighs its benefit. The optimistic approach assumes bad things won't happen and verifies at the end:
223	
224	1. **Read phase**: each transaction reads data and makes updates in a *private copy* (not committed to the database)
225	2. **Validate phase**: check whether the private updates conflict with any other concurrent transaction. If they pass: proceed. If they fail: restart the transaction
226	3. **Write phase**: commit the validated private copy to the database
227	
228	Advantage: no lock overhead for read-heavy workloads.  
229	Disadvantage: wasted work if validation fails frequently.
230	
231	---
232	
233	## Recovery
234	
235	Transactions provide one layer of protection. Additional recovery mechanisms protect against:
236	- System crash (power failure, OS crash)
237	- Disk damage
238	- User mistake
239	- Cyber attack
240	
241	**Transaction log:**
242	- Records every write operation, including before and after values
243	- Written to disk *before* the commit (write-ahead logging)
244	- Chained by transaction ID — allows replaying or undoing operations
245	- Stored on a *separate* device from the database (e.g., backup tape)
246	
247	**Recovery strategies:**
248	- **Checkpoint**: periodically record the current committed state to disk; on restart, replay only operations after the last checkpoint
249	- **Redo/undo**: redo committed but not-yet-persisted writes; undo uncommitted writes
250	
251	**Rule of thumb:** Prevention is the best medicine — redundant hardware, UPS, RAID, off-site backups, and regular checkpoint intervals reduce recovery time and data loss.
252	
253	---
254	
255	## Summary
256	
257	```
258	Physical layer (S5):
259	    Files → pages
260	    Heap: scan everything
261	    Sorted: range-friendly
262	    Index: targeted retrieval
263	      └── Hash: equality only, O(1)
264	      └── B+ Tree: equality + range, O(log n), dynamic
265	
266	Transaction layer (S6):
267	    ACID: Atomicity + Consistency + Isolation + Durability
268	    Schedules: serial (safe) → serializable (safe + concurrent)
269	    Concurrency control:
270	      ├── Locking (pessimistic): acquires locks; deadlock risk
271	      └── Optimistic (3-phase): assumes no conflict; validates before commit
272	    Recovery:
273	      ├── Transaction log (write-ahead, chained, on separate device)
274	      └── Checkpoint + redo/undo
275	```

10	
11	# Algorithm Complexity
12	
13	Algorithm complexity analysis answers the question: **how does resource consumption scale as input size grows?** It provides a machine-independent vocabulary for comparing algorithms and predicting performance under real-world loads. Time complexity (operations) and space complexity (memory) are both studied, but time is the primary focus.
14	
15	## Formal Definitions
16	
17	Let f(n) and g(n) be functions from positive integers to positive reals.
18	
19	### Big-Oh — O (Upper Bound)
20	
21	f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ > 0 such that:
22	
23	> f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
24	
25	"f grows **no faster than** g." Used for worst-case guarantees.
26	
27	### Big-Omega — Ω (Lower Bound)
28	
29	f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if there exist constants c > 0 and n₀ > 0 such that:
30	
31	> f(n) ≥ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
32	
33	"f grows **at least as fast as** g." Used for best-case / lower-bound proofs.
34	
35	### Big-Theta — Θ (Tight Bound)
36	
37	f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if f(n) = O(g(n)) AND f(n) = Ω(g(n)).
38	
39	"f grows **at exactly the same rate as** g (up to constants)." The most informative classification.
40	
41	## Common Complexity Classes
42	
43	Ordered from fastest to slowest:
44	
45	| Class | Name | Example algorithms |
46	|-------|------|--------------------|
47	| O(1) | Constant | Array index access, hash lookup |
48	| O(log n) | Logarithmic | Binary search, BST operations |
49	| O(n) | Linear | Linear search, array traversal |
50	| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | Merge sort, Heap sort |
51	| O(n²) | Quadratic | Bubble/Selection/Insertion sort |
52	| O(n³) | Cubic | Naive matrix multiplication |
53	| O(2^n) | Exponential | Subset enumeration, naive recursion |
54	| O(n!) | Factorial | Permutation generation, TSP brute force |
55	
56	Practical rule: O(n²) is acceptable for n ≤ ~10,000; O(n log n) for n ≤ ~10,000,000; O(n) for essentially any n.
57	
58	## Asymptotic Rules
59	
60	These rules simplify complexity analysis:
61	
62	1. **Drop constants**: 5n² → O(n²)
63	2. **Drop lower-order terms**: n² + n + 1 → O(n²)
64	3. **Sum rule**: O(f) + O(g) = O(max(f, g))
65	4. **Product rule**: O(f) · O(g) = O(f · g)
66	5. **Loop rule**: a loop with O(n) iterations and O(g(n)) body → O(n · g(n))
67	6. **Logarithm base doesn't matter**: O(log₂ n) = O(log₁₀ n) (differ by constant factor)
68	
69	## Best, Worst, and Average Case
70	
71	The **same algorithm** can have different complexities depending on input:
72	
73	- **Best case** (Ω): most favourable input (e.g., already-sorted array for Insertion Sort → O(n))
74	- **Worst case** (O): most adversarial input (e.g., reverse-sorted for Insertion Sort → O(n²))
75	- **Average case** (Θ): expected over all possible inputs — often hardest to compute, requires probabilistic analysis
76	- **Amortised**: average cost per operation over a sequence of operations (e.g., dynamic array append is O(1) amortised)
77	
78	Big-Oh in practice almost always means worst-case unless specified otherwise.
79	
80	## Master Theorem
81	
82	The Master Theorem solves recurrences of the form:
83	
84	> T(n) = a · T(n/b) + f(n)
85	
86	where a ≥ 1 (subproblems), b > 1 (size reduction factor), f(n) is the work per level.
87	
88	Let c_crit = log_b(a):
89	
90	| Case | Condition | Result |
91	|------|-----------|--------|
92	| **Case 1** | f(n) = O(n^(c_crit - ε)) | T(n) = Θ(n^c_crit) — recursion dominates |
93	| **Case 2** | f(n) = Θ(n^c_crit · log^k n) | T(n) = Θ(n^c_crit · log^(k+1) n) — balanced |
94	| **Case 3** | f(n) = Ω(n^(c_crit + ε)) + regularity | T(n) = Θ(f(n)) — combining step dominates |
95	
96	### Examples
97	
98	- **Merge Sort**: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → a=2, b=2, c_crit=1, f(n)=O(n) → Case 2 → **O(n log n)**
99	- **Binary Search**: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → a=1, b=2, c_crit=0, f(n)=O(1) → Case 2 → **O(log n)**
100	- **Strassen's Matrix Multiply**: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) → c_crit = log₂7 ≈ 2.81 > 2 → Case 1 → **O(n^2.81)**
101	
102	## Recursion Tree Method
103	
104	When the Master Theorem doesn't apply (unequal subproblem sizes, non-polynomial f(n)):
105	
106	1. Draw the recursion tree — each node is a subproblem, cost = work at that node
107	2. Sum the cost at each level
108	3. Multiply by the number of levels (tree height)
109	4. Sum across all levels
110	
111	The recursion tree method is also useful for gaining intuition before applying the Master Theorem.
112	
113	## Space Complexity
114	
115	Space complexity counts memory beyond the input:
116	- **In-place** algorithms use O(1) auxiliary space (Insertion Sort, Quick Sort)
117	- Merge Sort requires O(n) auxiliary space for the merge buffer
118	- Recursion depth contributes O(depth) stack space (DFS on a tree → O(h) where h is height)
119	
120	## See Also
121

123	- [[sorting-and-searching]] — applying complexity analysis to concrete algorithms
124	- [[graph-algorithms]] — O(V+E) analysis for traversal algorithms
125	- [[INF1008-data-structures-algorithms]] — source course

10	
11	# Data Structures Fundamentals
12	
13	A data structure is a way of organising data in memory to support efficient operations. The choice of data structure is the first and most consequential algorithmic decision: the right structure turns an O(n²) solution into O(n log n) or even O(1).
14	
15	## Abstract Data Types (ADTs)
16	
17	An **ADT** defines a data structure by its **operations and their contracts**, not its implementation. The same ADT (e.g., Stack) can be implemented as an array or a linked list — the ADT hides this choice from the user.
18	
19	Three things define an ADT:
20	1. The **data** it stores
21	2. The **operations** it supports
22	3. The **preconditions and postconditions** of each operation
23	
24	## Linear Data Structures
25	
26	### Arrays
27	
28	- Fixed-size (static) or resizable (dynamic/ArrayList)
29	- **O(1) random access** by index
30	- **O(n) insert/delete** at arbitrary position (shifting required)
31	- **O(1) append** at end (amortised for dynamic arrays)
32	- Best when: size is known, random access is frequent, cache locality matters
33	
34	### Stacks (LIFO)
35	
36	Last-In, First-Out. Operations:
37	- `push(x)` — add to top: O(1)
38	- `pop()` — remove from top: O(1)
39	- `peek()` — view top without removing: O(1)
40	
41	Applications: function call stack, undo/redo, expression evaluation (infix → postfix), DFS traversal, bracket matching.
42	
43	### Queues (FIFO)
44	
45	First-In, First-Out. Operations:
46	- `enqueue(x)` — add to rear: O(1)
47	- `dequeue()` — remove from front: O(1)
48	
49	Variants:
50	- **Circular Queue** — fixed-size array with wrap-around; avoids shifting
51	- **Double-Ended Queue (Deque)** — insert/delete at both ends
52	- **Priority Queue** — dequeue by priority, not arrival order (see Heaps below)
53	
54	Applications: BFS traversal, task scheduling, print spooling.
55	
56	### Linked Lists
57	
58	Each node contains data + a pointer to the next node. No contiguous memory required.
59	
60	| Type | Structure | Extra cost |
61	|------|-----------|-----------|
62	| **Singly Linked** | node → next | O(n) traversal only |
63	| **Doubly Linked** | prev ← node → next | O(1) backward traversal |
64	| **Circular** | tail → head | Loop detection algorithms |
65	
66	Operations:
67	- **Insert at head**: O(1)
68	- **Insert at tail**: O(1) with tail pointer, O(n) without
69	- **Search**: O(n)
70	- **Delete by value**: O(n) search + O(1) removal
71	
72	Best when: frequent insertion/deletion at arbitrary positions, size unknown, no random access needed.
73	
74	## Priority Queue & Heaps
75	
76	A **Priority Queue** is an ADT that always returns the element with the highest (or lowest) priority.
77	
78	A **Binary Heap** is the standard implementation:
79	- Complete binary tree stored as an array
80	- **Min-Heap**: parent ≤ children (root is minimum)
81	- **Max-Heap**: parent ≥ children (root is maximum)
82	
83	Operations:
84	- `insert`: O(log n) — add at end, bubble up
85	- `extract-min/max`: O(log n) — remove root, replace with last, bubble down
86	- `build-heap` from array: O(n) (not O(n log n) — amortised analysis)
87	
88	Applications: Dijkstra's algorithm, Prim's MST, Heap Sort, job scheduling.
89	
90	## Hash Tables
91	
92	A hash table maps keys to values in O(1) average time using a **hash function**.
93	
94	### Hash Function Properties
95	
96	A good hash function is:
97	- **Deterministic**: same input → same output
98	- **Uniform**: distributes keys evenly across buckets
99	- **Fast**: computed in O(1)
100	
101	### Collision Resolution
102	
103	Two keys can hash to the same slot (**collision**). Two resolution strategies:
104	
105	#### Chaining (Closed Addressing)
106	Each slot holds a linked list of all keys that hash there. Simple and handles high load factors. Worst case: O(n) if all keys hash to one slot.
107	
108	#### Open Addressing
109	All entries stored in the table itself. On collision, probe for the next empty slot:
110	- **Linear probing**: next slot +1, +2, ... (clustering problem)
111	- **Quadratic probing**: next slot +1², +2², ... (reduces primary clustering)
112	- **Double hashing**: next slot using a second hash function (best distribution)
113	
114	### Load Factor
115	
116	**Load factor** α = n/m (items/slots). Performance degrades as α → 1. Standard practice: resize (rehash) when α > 0.7. Chaining tolerates α > 1; open addressing requires α < 1.
117	
118	## Tree Structures
119	
120	### Binary Search Tree (BST)
121	
122	For every node: left subtree values < node < right subtree values.
123	
124	| Operation | Average | Worst (degenerate) |
125	|-----------|---------|-------------------|
126	| Search | O(log n) | O(n) |
127	| Insert | O(log n) | O(n) |
128	| Delete | O(log n) | O(n) |
129	
130	Worst case occurs when the tree is unbalanced (e.g., inserting sorted data creates a linked list). Balanced BSTs solve this.
131	
132	### AVL Trees
133	
134	Self-balancing BST (Adelson-Velsky and Landis, 1962). Maintains the **balance factor** (|height(left) - height(right)| ≤ 1) at every node.
135	
136	Rebalancing via **rotations** (single left, single right, double left-right, double right-left). All operations guaranteed O(log n). Stricter balance than Red-Black trees → faster lookups but slower inserts/deletes. Preferred for read-heavy workloads.
137	
138	### Red-Black Trees
139	
140	Self-balancing BST with five invariants:
141	1. Every node is red or black
142	2. Root is black
143	3. Leaves (NIL sentinels) are black
144	4. Red nodes have black children (no two consecutive reds)
145	5. All paths from a node to its descendant leaves have the same number of black nodes
146	
147	All operations O(log n). Less strictly balanced than AVL → faster inserts/deletes. Used in Java's `TreeMap`/`TreeSet`, Linux kernel scheduler, C++ `std::map`.
148	
149	### B-Trees
150	
151	Multi-way balanced search tree designed for **disk-resident data**. Each node holds multiple keys and has multiple children (order m means up to m children).
152	
153	Properties:
154	- All leaves at the same depth
155	- Each node (except root) has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children
156	- A node with k keys has k+1 children
157	
158	B-Trees minimise disk I/O by maximising data per node (one disk block = one node). Used in filesystem indices, database engines (MySQL InnoDB, PostgreSQL). B+ Trees (all data in leaves, leaves linked) are the standard variant in databases.
159	
160	## Complexity Comparison Table
161	
162	| Structure | Access | Search | Insert | Delete | Space |
163	|-----------|--------|--------|--------|--------|-------|
164	| Array | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
165	| Stack/Queue | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | O(n) |
166	| Singly Linked List | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) head | O(1) w/ptr | O(n) |
167	| Hash Table | N/A | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(1) avg | O(n) |
168	| BST | O(log n) avg | O(log n) avg | O(log n) avg | O(log n) avg | O(n) |
169	| AVL / Red-Black | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) |
170	| B-Tree | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) |
171	| Heap | O(1) min | O(n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) |
172	
173	## See Also
174	
175	- [[algorithm-complexity]] — formal complexity analysis
176	- [[sorting-and-searching]] — algorithms that operate on these structures
177	- [[graph-algorithms]] — graphs as generalisation of trees
178	- [[INF1008-data-structures-algorithms]] — source course

10	
11	# Sorting and Searching Algorithms
12	
13	Sorting and searching are among the most frequently performed operations in software. Understanding the trade-offs between algorithms — time complexity, space, stability, and practical constants — determines whether a feature runs in milliseconds or seconds.
14	
15	## Sorting Algorithms
16	
17	### Stability and In-Place Defined
18	
19	- **Stable**: equal elements retain their original relative order after sorting (important when sorting by secondary keys)
20	- **In-place**: uses O(1) auxiliary space (ignoring recursion stack)
21	
22	### Bubble Sort
23	
24	Repeatedly compare adjacent pairs; swap if out of order. Each full pass "bubbles" the largest unsorted element to its correct position.
25	
26	| Case | Complexity |
27	|------|-----------|
28	| Best (already sorted) | O(n) with early-exit flag |
29	| Average | O(n²) |
30	| Worst (reverse sorted) | O(n²) |
31	
32	Space: O(1). Stable: Yes. Practical use: essentially none — teaching tool only.
33	
34	### Selection Sort
35	
36	Find the minimum in the unsorted portion; swap it with the first unsorted element. Repeat.
37	
38	| Case | Complexity |
39	|------|-----------|
40	| All cases | O(n²) |
41	
42	Space: O(1). Stable: No (swapping breaks stability). Practical use: minimises swaps (useful when writes are expensive — e.g., flash memory).
43	
44	### Insertion Sort
45	
46	Build a sorted subarray from left to right by inserting each new element in the correct position.
47	
48	| Case | Complexity |
49	|------|-----------|
50	| Best (already sorted) | O(n) |
51	| Average | O(n²) |
52	| Worst (reverse sorted) | O(n²) |
53	
54	Space: O(1). Stable: Yes. Practical use: excellent for small arrays (n < 20) and nearly-sorted data. Used as the base case in Timsort and Introsort.
55	
56	### Merge Sort
57	
58	Divide-and-conquer: split array in half, recursively sort each half, merge the two sorted halves.
59	
60	| Case | Complexity |
61	|------|-----------|
62	| All cases | O(n log n) |
63	
64	Space: O(n) auxiliary for merge buffer. Stable: Yes.
65	
66	Practical use: preferred when stability is required and O(n) space is acceptable. Default for sorting linked lists (no random access needed). Java's `Arrays.sort()` for objects uses a variant (Timsort).
67	
68	**Merge step**: two-pointer technique — compare heads, emit smaller, advance that pointer. O(n) per level, O(log n) levels → O(n log n) total.
69	
70	### Quick Sort
71	
72	Divide-and-conquer: choose a **pivot**, partition array so all elements < pivot are left, all > pivot are right. Recursively sort each partition.
73	
74	| Case | Complexity |
75	|------|-----------|
76	| Best / Average | O(n log n) |
77	| Worst (already sorted, bad pivot) | O(n²) |
78	
79	Space: O(log n) avg recursion stack. Stable: No.
80	
81	Practical use: fastest in practice for most inputs due to cache locality and small constants. Java's `Arrays.sort()` for primitives; C's `qsort`. Mitigate worst case with **randomised pivot** or **median-of-three**.
82	
83	**Partition schemes**: Lomuto (simpler, slightly slower) vs Hoare (original, fewer swaps).
84	
85	## Complete Sorting Comparison Table
86	
87	| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Space | Stable | Notes |
88	|-----------|------|---------|-------|-------|--------|-------|
89	| Bubble | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | Yes | Teaching only |
90	| Selection | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | No | Min writes |
91	| Insertion | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | Yes | Small/nearly-sorted |
92	| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | Yes | Stable guarantee |
93	| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(log n) | No | Fastest in practice |
94	
95	## Searching Algorithms
96	
97	### Linear Search
98	
99	Check each element sequentially until found or exhausted.
100	
101	- Time: O(n) all cases
102	- Space: O(1)
103	- Works on: unsorted and sorted arrays, linked lists
104	- Use when: array is small, unsorted, or searched rarely
105	
106	### Binary Search
107	
108	On a **sorted** array: compare target with middle element; recurse on left or right half.
109	
110	- Time: O(log n)
111	- Space: O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive
112	- Requires: sorted, random-access array
113	- Use when: array is large and sorted (or can be kept sorted)
114	
115	```
116	low = 0, high = n-1
117	while low ≤ high:
118	    mid = (low + high) / 2
119	    if arr[mid] == target: return mid
120	    elif arr[mid] < target: low = mid + 1
121	    else: high = mid - 1
122	return NOT_FOUND
123	```
124	
125	Common bug: `(low + high) / 2` can overflow for large indices — use `low + (high - low) / 2`.
126	
127	## String Searching Algorithms
128	
129	String search finds the first occurrence of a pattern P (length m) in a text T (length n).
130	
131	### Brute Force
132	
133	Try every starting position in T; compare with P character by character.
134	
135	- Time: O(nm) worst case
136	- Space: O(1)
137	- Simple but slow for adversarial inputs (e.g., searching "aaab" in "aaaa...a")
138	
139	### KMP — Knuth-Morris-Pratt
140	
141	Preprocesses the pattern to build a **failure function** (also called partial match table / prefix function). When a mismatch occurs, instead of restarting from scratch, skip ahead using the failure function.
142	
143	**Failure function** `f[i]` = length of the longest proper prefix of `P[0..i]` that is also a suffix.
144	
145	Example for P = "ABABC":
146	- f[0]=0, f[1]=0, f[2]=1, f[3]=2, f[4]=0
147	
148	- Preprocessing: O(m)
149	- Search: O(n) — each character in T examined at most twice
150	- Total: **O(n + m)**
151	- Space: O(m) for failure function
152	
153	KMP is optimal for single-pattern search when the pattern has repeated structure.
154	
155	### Boyer-Moore
156	
157	Preprocesses the pattern using two heuristics:
158	1. **Bad Character Rule**: when mismatch at position j in pattern, shift pattern so the mismatched text character aligns with its rightmost occurrence in the pattern (or skip past the pattern if not found)
159	2. **Good Suffix Rule**: when mismatch after matching k characters, shift pattern so the matched suffix aligns with its next occurrence (or use a safe shift)
160	
161	Uses the larger of the two shifts. Scans **right-to-left** within the pattern.
162	
163	- Preprocessing: O(m + alphabet_size)
164	- Search: O(n/m) best case (sublinear!), O(nm) worst case
165	- Average: **O(n/m)** — faster than KMP for large alphabets and long patterns
166	
167	Boyer-Moore is preferred for text editors and search tools on natural language (large alphabet, long patterns). `grep` uses a variant (Boyer-Moore-Horspool).
168	
169	## When to Use Which Algorithm
170	
171	| Scenario | Recommendation |
172	|----------|---------------|
173	| n < 20, any order | Insertion Sort |
174	| Large n, stability required | Merge Sort |
175	| Large n, best average performance | Quick Sort (randomised pivot) |
176	| Already nearly sorted | Insertion Sort |
177	| External sort (disk) | Merge Sort |
178	| Array is sorted, find element | Binary Search |
179	| Array is unsorted, find element | Linear Search (or sort first) |
180	| Single pattern search, repeated prefixes | KMP |
181	| Single pattern, large alphabet, long pattern | Boyer-Moore |
182	
183	## See Also
184	
185	- [[algorithm-complexity]] — formal complexity analysis and Master Theorem
186	- [[data-structures-fundamentals]] — heaps enable Heap Sort; hash tables enable O(1) lookup
187	- [[graph-algorithms]] — DFS/BFS use stacks/queues
188	- [[INF1008-data-structures-algorithms]] — source course

10	
11	# Graph Algorithms
12	
13	Graphs are the most general relational data structure: they model anything with entities (nodes/vertices) and relationships (edges). Road networks, social networks, dependency graphs, state machines, and neural networks are all graphs. Graph algorithms are consequently among the most widely applied in computing.
14	
15	## Graph Fundamentals
16	
17	### Graph Types
18	
19	| Type | Description | Example |
20	|------|-------------|---------|
21	| **Undirected** | Edges have no direction (A-B = B-A) | Social friendships, road networks |
22	| **Directed (Digraph)** | Edges have direction (A→B ≠ B→A) | Web links, dependencies |
23	| **Weighted** | Edges carry numeric values | Road distances, network latency |
24	| **DAG** | Directed Acyclic Graph — no cycles | Task scheduling, build dependencies |
25	| **Tree** | Connected, undirected, acyclic | File systems, parse trees |
26	
27	### Graph Representations
28	
29	**Adjacency Matrix**: V×V matrix where cell [i][j] = 1 (or weight) if edge i→j exists.
30	- Space: O(V²)
31	- Edge lookup: O(1)
32	- Iterating neighbours: O(V)
33	- Best for: dense graphs (E ≈ V²), edge existence queries
34	
35	**Adjacency List**: array of V lists; list[i] contains all neighbours of vertex i.
36	- Space: O(V + E)
37	- Edge lookup: O(degree)
38	- Iterating neighbours: O(degree)
39	- Best for: sparse graphs (E << V²) — most real-world graphs
40	
41	## Traversal Algorithms
42	
43	### Depth-First Search (DFS)
44	
45	Explore as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Implemented with a **stack** (explicit or call stack via recursion).
46	
47	```
48	DFS(G, start):
49	    mark start as visited
50	    for each neighbour v of start:
51	        if v not visited:
52	            DFS(G, v)
53	```
54	
55	- Time: O(V + E) — each vertex and edge visited once
56	- Space: O(V) for visited set + O(V) recursion depth
57	- Applications:
58	  - Cycle detection
59	  - Topological sort
60	  - Strongly connected components (Kosaraju/Tarjan)
61	  - Maze solving
62	  - Finding connected components
63	
64	DFS on trees traverses nodes in pre/in/post-order depending on when the node is processed relative to its children.
65	
66	### Breadth-First Search (BFS)
67	
68	Explore all neighbours at distance k before any at distance k+1. Implemented with a **queue**.
69	
70	```
71	BFS(G, start):
72	    enqueue start; mark visited
73	    while queue not empty:
74	        v = dequeue
75	        for each neighbour u of v:
76	            if u not visited:
77	                mark u visited; enqueue u
78	```
79	
80	- Time: O(V + E)
81	- Space: O(V) for queue
82	- Applications:
83	  - **Shortest path in unweighted graphs** (BFS from source = shortest hop count)
84	  - Level-order traversal of trees
85	  - Finding connected components
86	  - Web crawlers (page = vertex, link = edge)
87	
88	Key property: BFS visits vertices in non-decreasing order of their distance from the source.
89	
90	## Topological Sort
91	
92	Only valid on **DAGs** (a cycle makes topological ordering impossible). A topological ordering is a linear sequence of vertices such that for every edge u→v, u appears before v.
93	
94	**DFS-based algorithm**:
95	1. Run DFS; when a vertex finishes (all descendants explored), push to a stack
96	2. Output stack in LIFO order
97	
98	Time: O(V + E). A DAG has at least one vertex with in-degree 0 (Kahn's algorithm alternative uses a queue and processes in-degree 0 vertices).
99	
100	Applications: Build systems (Makefile), compiler dependency resolution, course prerequisite ordering, task scheduling.
101	
102	## Minimum Spanning Trees (MST)
103	
104	Given a connected, undirected, weighted graph, an MST is a spanning tree (connects all V vertices) with **minimum total edge weight**. A graph has exactly one MST if all edge weights are distinct.
105	
106	### Prim's Algorithm
107	
108	Greedy: grow the MST one vertex at a time by always adding the minimum-weight edge that connects the current MST to a new vertex.
109	
110	1. Start with any vertex; mark it in MST
111	2. Maintain a priority queue of edges crossing the cut (MST ↔ non-MST)
112	3. Extract minimum-weight edge; add its new vertex to MST
113	4. Add all edges from new vertex to priority queue (if other endpoint not in MST)
114	5. Repeat until all vertices in MST
115	
116	- Time: O(E log V) with binary heap, O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heap
117	- Best for: **dense graphs** (processes edges efficiently)
118	
119	### Kruskal's Algorithm
120	
121	Greedy: sort all edges by weight; add each edge if it doesn't form a cycle.
122	
123	1. Sort all edges by weight: O(E log E)
124	2. For each edge (u, v) in order: if u and v in different components, add edge (use Union-Find)
125	3. Stop when V-1 edges added
126	
127	- Time: O(E log E) = O(E log V) for sorting
128	- Uses **Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)** for cycle detection: O(α(V)) per operation
129	- Best for: **sparse graphs**
130	
131	Both Prim's and Kruskal's produce the same MST (for graphs with unique edge weights).
132	
133	## Shortest Path Algorithms
134	
135	### Dijkstra's Algorithm
136	
137	Single-source shortest paths for graphs with **non-negative weights**.
138	
139	1. Initialise dist[source]=0, all others=∞
140	2. Maintain a min-heap of (distance, vertex) pairs
141	3. Extract minimum; for each neighbour v: if dist[u] + w(u,v) < dist[v], update dist[v] and push to heap
142	4. Repeat until heap empty
143	
144	- Time: O(E log V) with binary heap
145	- Space: O(V + E)
146	- Correctness: relies on non-negative weights — a negative edge would allow already-finalised vertices to be improved
147	
148	Applications: GPS navigation, network routing (OSPF protocol), game pathfinding (A* is Dijkstra with heuristic).
149	
150	### Bellman-Ford Algorithm
151	
152	Single-source shortest paths for graphs with **negative-weight edges** (but no negative-weight cycles).
153	
154	1. Initialise dist[source]=0, all others=∞
155	2. Repeat V-1 times: for every edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v]
156	3. Run one more iteration: if any dist[v] updates, a negative-weight cycle exists
157	
158	- Time: O(VE) — significantly slower than Dijkstra
159	- Space: O(V)
160	- Detects negative cycles (Dijkstra cannot)
161	
162	Applications: Currency arbitrage detection (negative cycle = profit cycle), routing protocols (distance-vector, e.g., RIP).
163	
164	## Algorithm Selection Guide
165	
166	| Problem | Algorithm | Condition |
167	|---------|-----------|-----------|
168	| Traverse all vertices | DFS or BFS | Any graph |
169	| Shortest path (unweighted) | BFS | Unweighted |
170	| Shortest path (non-negative weights) | Dijkstra | No negative edges |
171	| Shortest path (negative weights) | Bellman-Ford | No negative cycles |
172	| All-pairs shortest paths | Floyd-Warshall | Dense graphs |
173	| Minimum spanning tree (dense) | Prim's | Connected, undirected, weighted |
174	| Minimum spanning tree (sparse) | Kruskal's | Connected, undirected, weighted |
175	| Ordering with dependencies | Topological Sort | DAG only |
176	| Cycle detection | DFS | Any directed graph |
177	
178	## See Also
179	
180	- [[data-structures-fundamentals]] — heaps (Prim's/Dijkstra), union-find (Kruskal's), queues (BFS), stacks (DFS)
181	- [[algorithm-complexity]] — O(V+E), O(E log V) analysis
182	- [[INF1008-data-structures-algorithms]] — source course

10	
11	# Web Fundamentals (Internet, HTTP, DNS)
12	
13	Covers the history and architecture of the Internet and World Wide Web, the TCP/IP networking model, DNS resolution, URL structure, HTTP request/response, and web browser rendering.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. The Internet vs the Web
18	
19	| | Internet | World Wide Web |
20	|-|---------|---------------|
21	| **Created** | 1969 (ARPANET, US DoD) | 1989 (Tim Berners-Lee, CERN) |
22	| **What it is** | Global packet-switched network infrastructure | Application running *over* the Internet |
23	| **Core technologies** | TCP/IP | URL, HTTP, HTML |
24	
25	**Packet switching** (vs circuit switching): data is broken into independent packets that travel different routes and are reassembled at the destination. Efficient because packets share links; no dedicated circuit needed.
26	
27	**TCP/IP adopted** across all ARPANET in January 1983.
28	
29	---
30	
31	## 2. TCP/IP Network Model
32	
33	| Layer | Role | Protocols |
34	|-------|------|-----------|
35	| **Application** | Familiar protocols used by software | HTTP, FTP, SSH, DNS, SMTP, POP, IMAP |
36	| **Transport** | End-to-end delivery | TCP (reliable, ordered, ACKs) / UDP (fast, no guarantee) |
37	| **Internet (IP)** | Routing packets between networks; best-effort | IPv4, IPv6 |
38	| **Link** | Physical transmission; error detection | MAC addresses, Ethernet, Wi-Fi |
39	
40	**TCP** guarantees arrival and ordering via sequence numbers and acknowledgements. Lost packets are retransmitted.
41	
42	**UDP** trades reliability for speed — used in streaming, VoIP, gaming, DNS.
43	
44	**IPv4**: four 8-bit integers (`192.168.1.1`) — address space exhausted in 2011.
45	**IPv6**: eight 16-bit integers — vastly larger space.
46	**PAT (Port Address Translation)**: allows multiple devices to share one IPv4 address.
47	
48	---
49	
50	## 3. DNS — Domain Name System
51	
52	Translates human-readable hostnames to IP addresses. Evolved from a simple `hosts` file to a distributed, hierarchical system.
53	
54	### Domain Name Structure
55	
56	- **gTLD** (Generic): `.com`, `.net`, `.org`, `.gov`, `.edu`; new TLDs since 2012 (`.art`, `.cash`, …)
57	- **ccTLD** (Country Code): `.sg`, `.uk`, `.ca`
58	- **IDN** (Internationalised): non-ASCII characters (deployed 2009)
59	- **ICANN** oversees TLD management and accredits registrars.
60	
61	### DNS Resolution — 10-Step Process
62	
63	1. Client makes domain request
64	2. Check local DNS cache
65	3. If not cached → query primary DNS server
66	4. Primary DNS queries Root Name Server
67	5. Root returns TLD server address
68	6. DNS server queries TLD server
69	7. TLD returns Authoritative DNS Server addresses
70	8. DNS server queries Authoritative DNS Server
71	9. IP address returned to DNS server
72	10. Client makes request to the resolved IP
73	
74	---
75	
76	## 4. URLs
77	
78	Structure: `protocol://domain[:port][/path][?query][#fragment]`
79	
80	| Component | Description | Example |
81	|-----------|-------------|---------|
82	| Protocol | Connection type | `https://` |
83	| Domain | Server address | `www.example.com` |
84	| Port | Optional (default HTTP=80, HTTPS=443) | `:8080` |
85	| Path | File or directory on server | `/blog/post` |
86	| Query string | Key-value parameters | `?id=42&lang=en` |
87	| Fragment | Page section anchor | `#section2` |
88	
89	**Relative URL types**:
90	
91	| Type | Syntax |
92	|------|--------|
93	| Same directory | `file.html` |
94	| Child directory | `subdir/file.html` |
95	| Parent directory | `../file.html` |
96	| Root reference | `/path/file.html` |
97	
98	---
99	
100	## 5. HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol
101	
102	### Request Methods
103	
104	| Method | Use |
105	|--------|-----|
106	| **GET** | Retrieve a resource; data in URL query string |
107	| **POST** | Send data (forms); data in request body |
108	| **HEAD** | Like GET but headers only |
109	| **PUT** | Update/replace a resource |
110	| **DELETE** | Delete a resource |
111	
112	| Property | GET | POST |
113	|----------|-----|------|
114	| Data location | URL | Body |
115	| Bookmarkable | Yes | No |
116	| Cached | Yes | No |
117	| Binary data | No | Yes |
118	| Use case | Search/filtering | Login/submission |
119	
120	**Safety and idempotency**: GET is both safe and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent (same result if repeated) but not safe; POST is neither.
121	
122	### Response Status Codes
123	
124	| Code | Meaning |
125	|------|---------|
126	| 200 OK | Successful |
127	| 301 Moved Permanently | Permanent redirect |
128	| 304 Not Modified | Cached version is current |
129	| 401 Unauthorized | Authentication required |
130	| 404 Not Found | Resource not found |
131	| 414 URI Too Long | Too much data in URL |
132	| 500 Internal Server Error | Server-side error |
133	
134	### HTTP Headers
135	
136	- **Request**: `Host`, `User-Agent`, cache directives
137	- **Response**: `Server`, `Last-Modified`, `Content-Type`, encoding
138	
139	---
140	
141	## 6. Browser Rendering
142	
143	When a browser receives an HTML document it:
144	1. Parses HTML → finds all referenced resources (CSS, JS, images)
145	2. Downloads resources (can be parallelised)
146	3. Applies CSS → layout
147	4. Renders to screen
148	
149	### Key Performance Metrics
150	
151	| Metric | Meaning |
152	|--------|---------|
153	| **TTFB** | Time to First Byte |
154	| **FP** | First Paint |
155	| **FCP** | First Contentful Paint |
156	| **LCP** | Largest Contentful Paint |
157	| **TTI** | Time to Interactive |
158	| **CLS** | Cumulative Layout Shift |
159	
160	---
161	
162	## 7. Web Application Stacks
163	
164	| Stack | Components |
165	|-------|-----------|
166	| **LAMP** | Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP |
167	| **MERN** | MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js |
168	| **WISA** | Windows, IIS, SQL Server, ASP.NET |
169	| **JAM** | JavaScript, APIs, Markup (static sites) |
170	
171	---
172	
173	## 8. Client-Server Architecture
174	
175	- **Clients**: devices varying in OS, speed, screen size, memory (browsers, phones, tablets)
176	- **Servers**: respond to HTTP requests — types include Web, Application, Database, Mail, Media, Authentication
177	- **Server farms**: multiple servers + load balancers + failover for reliability and scale
178	- **Cloud services**: elastic provisioning — scale on demand
179	
180	**Web 2.0** shifted the web from read-only (static HTML) to interactive — users contribute content; logic migrated from server to browser (JavaScript).
181	
182	---
183	
184	## See Also
185	
186	- [[concepts/html-and-css|HTML and CSS]] — markup and styling layer built on top of HTTP
187	- [[concepts/javascript-fundamentals|JavaScript Fundamentals]] — client-side programming
188	- [[concepts/server-side-web-development|Server-Side Web Development]] — PHP, Node.js, databases
189	- [[concepts/web-security-and-devops|Web Security and DevOps]] — HTTPS, authentication, hosting
190	- [[sources/INF1005-web-systems-technologies|INF1005 Source Page]]

9	---
10	
11	# Web Security and DevOps
12	
13	Covers the CIA triad, STRIDE threat model, authentication strategies, cryptography, TLS/HTTPS, common attack vectors (SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, brute force, DoS), hosting options, cloud service models, CI/CD, and DNS administration.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. Information Security Core Concepts
18	
19	### CIA Triad
20	
21	| Property | Meaning |
22	|----------|---------|
23	| **Confidentiality** | Protect data from unauthorised access |
24	| **Integrity** | Ensure data is accurate and unaltered |
25	| **Availability** | Ensure systems are accessible when needed |
26	
27	### STRIDE Threat Model (Microsoft)
28	
29	| Letter | Threat | Description |
30	|--------|--------|-------------|
31	| **S** | Spoofing | Attacker uses someone else's credentials |
32	| **T** | Tampering | Unauthorised modification of data |
33	| **R** | Repudiation | Removing traces of an attack; denying actions |
34	| **I** | Information Disclosure | Unauthorised access to sensitive data |
35	| **D** | Denial of Service | Preventing legitimate access to a system |
36	| **E** | Elevation of Privilege | Gaining unauthorised system privileges |
37	
38	---
39	
40	## 2. Authentication and Authorisation
41	
42	**Authentication** = verifying *who you are*.
43	**Authorisation** = determining *what you are allowed to do*.
44	
45	### Authentication Factors
46	
47	| Factor | Type |
48	|--------|------|
49	| **Knowledge** | Something you know — password, PIN |
50	| **Ownership** | Something you have — token, phone, hardware key |
51	| **Inherence** | Something you are — fingerprint, face scan |
52	
53	**MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)**: requires two distinct factors.
54	
55	### Web Authentication Strategies
56	
57	| Strategy | Description | Notes |
58	|----------|-------------|-------|
59	| **HTTP Basic Auth** | Browser popup; credentials in request header | Simple, but credentials sent with every request |
60	| **Form-Based Auth** | Custom HTML form; POST to server; session cookies | Most common; requires HTTPS |
61	| **Token Auth (Bearer/JWT)** | Stateless tokens in `Authorization` header | Used for REST APIs; no server-side session |
62	| **Third-Party Auth (OAuth)** | "Sign in with Google/GitHub" | Delegates auth to trusted provider |
63	
64	---
65	
66	## 3. Cryptography
67	
68	### Symmetric Encryption
69	
70	Same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast but requires secure key distribution.
71	- **AES** (Advanced Encryption Standard) — current standard.
72	
73	### Asymmetric (Public Key) Cryptography
74	
75	Two mathematically linked keys:
76	- **Public key** — shared openly; used to encrypt or verify
77	- **Private key** — kept secret; used to decrypt or sign
78	
79	Solves the key distribution problem. Used in TLS and digital signatures.
80	
81	### Digital Signatures
82	
83	Validate **authenticity**, **integrity**, and **non-repudiation** of a message. Signed with private key; verified with public key.
84	
85	### TLS / HTTPS
86	
87	**TLS** (Transport Layer Security) — successor to SSL. **HTTPS** = HTTP over TLS — encrypts all data in transit.
88	
89	Requires an **SSL/TLS certificate** issued by a **Certificate Authority (CA)**.
90	
91	| Certificate Type | Verification | Trust Level |
92	|-----------------|-------------|-------------|
93	| **DV** (Domain-Validated) | Domain ownership only | Basic |
94	| **OV** (Organisation-Validated) | Organisation identity | Higher |
95	| **EV** (Extended Validation) | Strictest verification | Highest; used by banks |
96	
97	---
98	
99	## 4. Credential Storage
100	
101	```php
102	// BAD: Plain-text passwords
103	$password = "mypassword";
104	
105	// BAD: MD5 — fast, vulnerable to rainbow tables
106	$hash = md5($password);
107	
108	// GOOD: bcrypt via PHP's built-in function
109	$hash = password_hash($password, PASSWORD_BCRYPT);
110	$valid = password_verify($inputPassword, $storedHash);
111	```
112	
113	**Salting**: adding unique random noise to each password before hashing. Prevents rainbow table attacks — even identical passwords produce different hashes.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 5. Common Attack Vectors
118	
119	### SQL Injection
120	
121	Malicious SQL code embedded in user input:
122	
123	```sql
124	-- Attacker input: ' OR '1'='1
125	SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='' OR '1'='1'; -- Always true
126	```
127	
128	**Defence**: use **prepared statements / parameterised queries** (never string-concatenate user input into SQL).
129	
130	```php
131	$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :id");
132	$stmt->bindValue(':id', $_GET['id']);
133	$stmt->execute();
134	```
135	
136	---
137	
138	### Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
139	
140	Malicious script injected into a trusted page, executed in victims' browsers.
141	
142	| Type | How |
143	|------|-----|
144	| **Reflected XSS** | Script returned immediately in server response (e.g., search result page) |
145	| **Stored XSS** | Script stored in database; affects all visitors to that page |
146	
147	**Defence**:
148	- Escape all output with `htmlspecialchars()` in PHP (or equivalent)
149	- Sanitise all user input before storing
150	- Set **Content Security Policy (CSP)** headers
151	- Avoid using `innerHTML` with user-controlled data in JavaScript
152	
153	```php
154	$safe = htmlspecialchars($_POST["comment"]);
155	```
156	
157	---
158	
159	### Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
160	
161	Forces authenticated users to execute unwanted actions on a site where they are logged in.
162	
163	**Defence**: include a unique, unpredictable **CSRF token** in every state-changing form:
164	
165	```html
166	<input type="hidden" name="csrf-token" value="randomUniqueToken123">
167	```
168	
169	Server validates the token before processing the request.
170	
171	---
172	
173	### Brute-Force Attacks
174	
175	Automated password guessing.
176	
177	**Defences**: rate limiting, account lockout after N failed attempts, CAPTCHA, intrusion detection systems.
178	
179	---
180	
181	### Denial of Service (DoS / DDoS)
182	
183	Overloading a server with illegitimate requests, preventing real users from accessing it.
184	
185	**Defences**: rate limiting, CDN (Content Delivery Network), load balancers, DDoS protection services (e.g., Cloudflare).
186	
187	---
188	
189	### Security Misconfiguration
190	
191	- Out-of-date server software
192	- Default credentials not changed
